South Korean, U.S. and Japanese Foreign Ministers to Meet in U.S. on G20 Sidelines; Korean Peninsula Talks on Agenda?
The foreign ministers of South Korea, the United States and Japan will meet in Atlanta, Georgia, on October 30 (local time). About a month after their last meeting, they are expected to discuss issues concerning the Korean Peninsula, regional and global affairs, and ways to cooperate on energy and economic security.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun (right), U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio (left), and Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu (center) walk together after meeting for a trilateral foreign ministers' meeting in New York on September 21 (local time). Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
View original image
According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Minister Cho Hyun is scheduled to hold a trilateral meeting with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) Foreign Ministers' Meeting that afternoon.
The three foreign ministers are meeting about a month after their September 21 meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. They also met in July on the sidelines of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) summit in Türkiye and the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) in the Philippines.
At this meeting, they are expected to discuss the situation on the Korean Peninsula, including North Korea's recent military provocations such as ballistic missile launches and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's visit to China, as well as ways for the three countries to coordinate.
North Korea is continuing its shows of force while touting advances in its weapons systems. On October 30, North Korea said through the Korean Central News Agency that it had staged a show of force the previous day involving suicide drones, cruise missiles and 600-mm multiple rocket launchers. The Joint Chiefs of Staff also detected around 10 missiles, including short-range ballistic missiles, launched the previous day from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea.
Whether the ministers will also discuss conditions for resuming U.S.-North Korea talks is drawing attention. The Lee Jaemyung administration has expressed its willingness to serve as a "pacesetter" for such talks, so the ministers may exchange views on ways to bring North Korea back to the negotiating table. At a parliamentary audit by the National Assembly's Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee on October 27, Cho said, "I think a U.S.-North Korea summit could serve as a catalyst for breaking the current impasse."
At their meeting last month, the three foreign ministers reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea and called on it to return to dialogue.
Minister Cho is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with major European countries on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting. A separate bilateral meeting between the South Korean and U.S. foreign ministers is also being arranged. Requests from various countries to meet with the United States, the G20 host, have been piling up, and, given Secretary Rubio's schedule, the possibility of a brief meeting remains open, according to reports.

high_priority_articles.full_text: Australia has given greater priority to national security and economic resilience in an update to its critical minerals strategy, a shift from a 2023 edition that placed heavier emphasis on climate goals. It also highlights the importance of international partnerships and targets government efforts where they can have the greatest comparative advantage by expanding domestic processing and refining. The 2026 update to the Critical Minerals Strategy 2023–2030 keeps the 2030 vision and six focus areas, but critical minerals, it says, "are no longer a resources issue". It announces no new money, restating existing commitments including the AUD 17.5 billion (USD 12.3 billion) Production Tax Incentive and a AUD 5 billion (USD 3.5 billion) Critical Minerals Facility. The update was discussed by Australian mining minister Madeline King at the International Mining and Resources Conference (IMARC) in Sydney on 27–29 October, where Benchmark lithium product director Cam Perks was in attendance.

high_priority_articles.title: US Pushes Stronger ASEAN Naval Cooperation as South China Sea Disputes Raise Regional Security Concerns - Wake Up Singapore
high_priority_articles.summary: US Pushes Stronger ASEAN Naval Cooperation as South China Sea Disputes Raise Regional Security Concerns  Wake Up Singapore
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Philippines: The United States is seeking closer military cooperation with Southeast Asian countries, with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth proposing a new defence framework and stronger joint naval operations amid continuing tensions in the South China Sea.
Hegseth made the proposal during the ASEAN-US Defence Ministers’ Informal Meeting in Cebu on Wednesday, where he called for greater coordination between regional armed forces.
Footage shows Philippine Defence Secretary Gilbert Teodoro welcoming Hegseth before the two officials joined other ASEAN defence ministers for discussions and group photographs.
Washington’s proposed plans include improving maritime surveillance, expanding joint military exercises and strengthening cooperation between regional navies.
“Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together, and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict,” Hegseth said.
He also reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to working with Southeast Asian countries to maintain regional stability.
“The United States is a proud Pacific nation, and alongside our ASEAN partners, we are resolved to deliver peace through strength, peace, prosperity and sovereignty for all member nations based on mutual respect,” he added.
US Proposes New Defence Framework
One of the key proposals discussed was a new US-ASEAN defence cooperation framework designed to guide military collaboration over the coming years.
The initiative comes as Southeast Asian nations prepare for further regional defence discussions, with Singapore scheduled to chair the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) in 2027.
The proposed framework could provide a platform for expanding cooperation in maritime security, military training and coordination between armed forces.
Hegseth also highlighted the importance of building stronger relationships between Washington and its Southeast Asian partners as regional security challenges continue.
Philippines Backs Stronger US Military Presence
Philippine Defence Secretary Gilbert Teodoro welcomed Washington’s continued involvement in Southeast Asian security, describing a strong US presence as important for regional peace and stability.
He also stressed the importance of maintaining freedom of navigation, particularly for countries that depend on international maritime routes for trade and economic activity.
“The Philippines hopes to build on these efforts in the years to come. Because all of us have relied and will continue to rely on freedom of navigation for the security, prosperity and resilience of our people,” Teodoro said.
The meeting also coincided with the 80th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the Philippines and the United States.
Hegseth further pointed to the 50th anniversary of formal US-ASEAN relations in 2027, describing it as another opportunity to strengthen military partnerships.
South China Sea Remains A Major Concern
The discussions come amid repeated confrontations in the disputed South China Sea, where several countries have overlapping territorial claims.
China claims large areas of the waterway, while the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia also maintain claims over parts of the region.
The Philippines and China have repeatedly clashed over access to contested waters, making maritime security a major concern for governments across Southeast Asia.
The latest US proposal highlights Washington’s efforts to expand its defence partnerships in the region as disputes over navigation and territorial claims continue.
With Singapore preparing to chair the ADMM in 2027, regional defence cooperation is expected to remain an important topic for ASEAN members and their international partners.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has reported that it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region.
The drone was “intercepted and destroyed” on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post. It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate.
A Houthi spokesperson denied targeting the Muslim holy city or surrounding region, reiterating that the group’s cross-border attacks remain strictly focused on Saudi energy and military infrastructure.
The Saudi-led coalition has previously accused the Houthis of launching drones towards Islam’s two holiest cities: Mecca and Medina.
“Our operations target [Saudi] oil facilities and military bases, and there is no longer anyone in this world who believes these fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal Al Saud regime,” the Houthi spokesman wrote.
Escalating hostilities
The opposing claims come as hostilities continue with no sign of slowing, and humanitarian agencies warn of worsening conditions for civilians.
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region. It later said two ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, were also intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Malki reported early on Friday that the coalition’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile that targeted western Saudi Arabia.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported later that coalition air attacks were targeting the Mahliyah district in Marib, Haifan in Taiz, and Huwaishan in al-Jawf in the country.
Al Jazeera Arabic’s Hadeel al-Yamani reported from Taiz that fighting along the front lines was persisting.
The governor of Taiz said the city was suffering heavy shelling, with residential neighbourhoods taking hits.
“Aircraft can be heard frequently over the city, which remains under a suffocating siege, with no medical supplies, water or fuel getting in,” al-Yamani reported.
“On the western front, there were intermittent clashes around dawn. The northern fronts were relatively calm, but still saw sporadic fighting. There has been a notable escalation in hostilities around Jabal Saber and Jabal Habashi,” he said.

high_priority_articles.summary: TSMC Weighs Rare-Earth-Free Motors Amid China's Export Controls, Moves to Diversify Supply Chain [Taiwan Chip News]  아시아경제
high_priority_articles.full_text:
TSMC Weighs Rare-Earth-Free Motors Amid China's Export Controls, Moves to Diversify Supply Chain [Taiwan Chip News]
TSMC Considers Replacing Rare-Earth Motors
Export Controls Threaten Semiconductor Component Supply Chains
Taiwanese Companies Pursue Alternative Technologies
Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s largest foundry, is considering adopting rare-earth-free motors to reduce supply chain risks arising from China’s export restrictions on rare earths. As even key components used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment become targets for supply chain diversification, Taiwanese companies are accelerating the development and commercialization of alternative technologies.
According to Taiwan’s Economic Daily News, Reuters and other sources on October 31, TSMC recently asked suppliers whether rare-earth-free motors could be used in its factory automation equipment. The move is intended to prepare for possible disruptions to component procurement caused by China’s export restrictions on rare earths. TSMC is including components that use rare earths in its equipment supply chain risk management and assessing whether they can be replaced.
In April 2025, China imposed export controls on items related to seven rare earths: samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium. In October of the same year, it announced measures to further expand the controls to cover additional rare earths, as well as related equipment and technologies. The scope of the controls extended beyond rare-earth materials to include technologies related to permanent magnet manufacturing, increasing uncertainty across global supply chains.
China postponed until November 10, 2026, the implementation of some measures announced in October to expand the controls. However, existing export controls remain in place, increasing the need for companies to diversify their supply chains. Since rare earths are key materials for high-performance permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, robots and industrial automation equipment, the semiconductor industry is also closely monitoring their potential impact on the procurement of manufacturing equipment components. The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that “defense and semiconductor supply chains could also be particularly affected if export licenses for components containing rare earth elements are delayed or denied.”
Adopting rare-earth-free motors requires more than simply replacing the magnets in existing motors. Their efficiency, torque, control performance and reliability must also meet the requirements of semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
In response, semiconductor component companies in Taiwan are drawing on their respective strengths in materials, motor design, and drive and control technologies to develop alternatives. As uncertainty over rare-earth supplies spills over into procurement challenges for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, companies are moving to secure related technologies and component supply chains ahead of time. China Steel is pursuing the development of alternative motors based on its materials technologies, including electrical steel sheets, while Fukuta is drawing on its motor design and manufacturing expertise. Shuo Yang is exploring ways to apply motor technologies that do not use rare-earth magnets, such as reluctance motors, in industrial equipment and cooling systems for AI data centers.
The Taiwanese government is also working to establish a domestic rare-earth supply chain. The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) currently operates a rare-earth pilot production line and, with government support, is moving forward with plans to build a separate demonstration production facility. The facility is targeted for completion by the end of 2028, with annual production of 500 tons of rare earths by the end of 2030. The Taiwanese government plans to use it to meet about 50% of the island’s domestic demand for rare earths.

high_priority_articles.title: Asim Munir | Biography, Army Chief, Pakistan, India, Afghanistan, Balochistan, & Kashmir - Britannica
high_priority_articles.summary: Asim Munir | Biography, Army Chief, Pakistan, India, Afghanistan, Balochistan, & Kashmir  Britannica
high_priority_articles.full_text:
(born 1968?, Rawalpindi?, Pakistan) is a Pakistani military officer who has served as the chief of Army Staff of Pakistan since November 2022. An intelligence veteran, he has also served as the director general of Military Intelligence (MI) and the director general of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), the country’s top intelligence agency. In May 2025 he was promoted to the rank of Field Marshal, the highest military rank in the country, while continuing to serve as the chief of Army Staff. He is the second person in Pakistan’s history to hold this rank after Mohammad Ayub Khan in 1959. In November 2025 the Parliament of Pakistan passed the 27th constitutional amendment, which elevated Munir to the newly created post of chief of defense forces, allowing him to oversee all branches of the armed forces such as the Air Force and Navy. The amendment also allows him to retain the privileges associated with his rank as Field Marshal indefinitely, effectively granting him lifelong immunity from criminal prosecution.
Early life and military career
Although Munir’s date and place of birth are unclear, media reports indicate he was born in 1968 in Rawalpindi, the location of the army’s headquarters and the capital of Pakistan from 1959 to 1969. His father was a schoolteacher and an imam (Muslim cleric). In 1986 Munir graduated from the Officers Training School at Mangla, Pakistan, where he was awarded the Sword of Honour for being the top cadet of his cohort. He was subsequently commissioned into the Pakistan Army and was posted to the Frontier Force Regiment, an infantry unit. He holds a master’s degree from the National Defence University in Islamabad, and he completed courses from military institutions in Japan and Malaysia. At one point in his career Munir served as a military attaché in Saudi Arabia. During this time he reportedly learned the Qurʾān and became a ḥāfiẓ—a title given to those who can recite every passage in the Qurʾān from memory, signifying immense spiritual achievement.
After several years of service and holding various leadership positions in the army, Munir became director general of MI in 2017. In October 2018 he was appointed director general of the ISI but was removed after about eight months, reportedly on Prime Minister Imran Khan’s insistence. The reason for his removal was not made public, although media reports speculated about tensions between the two.
In February 2019, while Munir was serving as ISI chief, tensions between India and Pakistan deteriorated after a suicide bomber rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into an Indian Central Reserve Police Force convoy in Pulwama, Jammu and Kashmir, killing some 40 security personnel. India’s government claimed that Pakistan was responsible for overseeing the attack, alleging that the Pakistan-based group Jaish-e-Mohammed—which claimed responsibility—received support from the ISI. Pakistan denied any role in the attack. The Indian military retaliated with air strikes on what it said was a Jaish-e-Mohammed training camp in Balakot, Pakistan.
Chief of Army Staff
In November 2022 Pakistani Pres. Arif Alvi appointed Munir as the country’s chief of Army Staff, the most influential position in both security and politics in Pakistan. The appointment came amid escalating tensions with former prime minister Khan, who had been ousted via a no-confidence motion in April and was shot in the leg in an apparent assassination attempt just weeks before Munir took office. In May 2023 Khan was arrested amid a flurry of legal cases, including corruption charges, shortly after accusing a top military officer of orchestrating the November attack, an accusation that the military publicly dismissed as “highly irresponsible and baseless.”
As army chief, Munir has taken a firm, often nationalist, stance on pressing security issues. He has emphasized a security-first approach, seeking to establish Pakistan as a regional military power. Focused on countering internal and external security threats, his approach combines assertive defense diplomacy—particularly toward India and Afghanistan—with strategic neutrality and economic self-reliance.
Munir has consistently blamed the Taliban government in Afghanistan for allowing Tehreek-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP; a group banned in Pakistan and designated as a terrorist organization by countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States) militants to launch attacks against Pakistan from Afghan territory. Tensions between the two neighbors surged in March 2024 after several militant groups, including the TTP, launched a series of terrorist attacks on China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) infrastructure, killing several Chinese nationals. In December the TTP claimed responsibility for an attack on a Pakistani military outpost in northwestern Pakistan near the country’s border with Afghanistan. The Pakistan military retaliated with air strikes against militant groups in Afghanistan. In January 2025 Munir asserted that the presence of TTP in Afghanistan was a major irritant in the two countries’ ties and called on the Taliban to end “the spread of terrorism in Pakistan from across the border.” Tensions came to a head in October when Pakistan carried out an air strike in Kabul that it said targeted the leader of the TTP, leading to skirmishes between the two countries (see Afghanistan-Pakistan Conflict [2025]). The Taliban denied the accusations of allowing safe haven for the TTP.
Munir has condemned the insurgency in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, where militants have pursued a separatist agenda for decades. In January 2024 Iran launched cross-border strikes against what it said were militant camps in Balochistan. Munir condemned the attacks and vowed to retaliate. A few days later Pakistan launched missile strikes on targets in Iran’s Sīstān va Balūchestān province. The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA)—which is designated as a terrorist organization by countries such as Pakistan, the United States, and the United Kingdom—was involved in attacks targeting CPEC infrastructure in 2024. Following a deadly train hijacking in March 2025 that left more than 20 passengers dead, for which the BLA claimed responsibility, Munir vowed to defeat separatist networks and facilitators operating in the region. Despite Balochistan’s location on the opposite side of Pakistan from India, Pakistan’s army claimed that India was supporting the insurgents, an allegation denied by India.
Munir has reiterated his country’s traditional position on Kashmir, supporting self-determination for the people of the region. He has vowed that Kashmir will one day become part of Pakistan and has referred to Kashmir as Pakistan’s “jugular vein.” In April 2025 fresh tensions between India and Pakistan erupted after a terrorist attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir, killed 26 people, mostly tourists. India blamed Pakistan for facilitating the attack, citing a history of supporting insurgency in the region and its alleged support for previous terrorist attacks against Indian civilians and soldiers. Pakistan rejected the accusations, claiming the group that India accused of orchestrating the attack was defunct and calling for an independent investigation. As tensions escalated between the two countries, Munir warned that Pakistan would retaliate swiftly to any Indian military action. On May 7, 2025, India launched multiple missile strikes on what it said were militant targets in Pakistan. This led to a sharp escalation, with exchanges from both sides, before a ceasefire was eventually agreed to.

high_priority_articles.title: Industry seeks extension of PLI scheme for white goods: EPACK Durable MD - electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com
high_priority_articles.summary: Industry seeks extension of PLI scheme for white goods: EPACK Durable MD  electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: A top executive at homegrown EPACK Durable said the consumer durables makers have sought an extension of the production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for white goods, as revenue threshold was too stringent.Ajay DD Singhania, managing director (MD), EPACK Durable, told ETElectronicsWorld in an interview.
The government had envisioned a fivefold jump in revenue in the fourth year under the scheme, which has not yet materialised, Singhania said. “Each investment has a cycle, and revenue generation takes time…many people could not take advantage despite having invested.”
The PLI scheme for white goods has an outlay of ₹6,238 crore, with an implementation timeline from FY2021-22 to FY2028-29. It provides a 4-6% financial incentive on the incremental sales of locally manufactured components over a baseline year, and envisions increasing domestic value addition from 15-20% to 75-80%.
“The government is still left with a substantial budget…," he said, underscoring that the industry together with EPACK Durable has recommended the government to extend the PLI for 2-3 years more.
Till now, it has attracted an investment commitment of ₹11,198 crore from 85 approved beneficiaries, which is expected to lead to an expected production value of ₹1.90 lakh crore during the scheme period.
EPACK Durable says it is the second-largest room air conditioner (RAC) original design manufacturer (ODM) in India. It manufactures fully assembled ACs, including indoor and outdoor units, and window ACs, as well as RAC components for various brands such as Voltas, Blue Star, Haier Appliances India, Carrier Midea India, Havells India, Godrej & Boyce, and supplies components to LG Electronics India.
“We have formed a technology joint venture (JV) with China’s Hisense, wherein we are bringing Hisense's global tech products to India, including a front-load washing machine,” Singhania said, adding that Hisense launched domestically made ACs in January this year.
The listed company reported a 34% year-on-year increase in the Q1FY27 revenue to ₹886 crore, supported by broad-based growth across its portfolio.
The company, during a post-earnings conference call with analysts, said that EPACK’s core RAC business continued to grow strongly, while small and large domestic appliances as well as components scaled up at an “encouraging pace”, led by air fryers and washing machines.

high_priority_articles.title: Hormuz shipping crisis deepens as Iran reports tanker fires, Houthis target Saudi oil facilities - The News Pakistan
high_priority_articles.summary: Hormuz shipping crisis deepens as Iran reports tanker fires, Houthis target Saudi oil facilities  The News Pakistan
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said four oil tankers had caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, while separate maritime security reports pointed to further attacks on commercial shipping, as the widening conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel continued to threaten critical energy infrastructure across the Gulf.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tankers had attempted to navigate routes it described as unauthorised. In its latest statement, it reported that a fourth vessel, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil, had struck a naval mine, suffered a powerful explosion and caught fire, Iranian state media reported on Friday.
An earlier IRGC Navy statement had reported that another tanker carrying two million barrels of crude had struck a mine.
Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian military's account.
Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it had received a report that a crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while completing an outbound transit through the strait.
In an earlier incident report, UKMTO said a vessel had been hit on its port side about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran's Lavan Island, triggering a fire on board. Its crew were reported safe, with no environmental impact.
It was not immediately clear whether the vessels involved in the UKMTO reports were among the four tankers cited by Iran.
In a separate report on Friday, Reuters said UKMTO had reported a tanker being struck by explosive devices attached to a small boat, in what maritime sources described as the first known successful limpet-mine attack in the waterway since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
The incidents underline the growing dangers to commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage connecting the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea through which around a fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the conflict.
Iranian state media also reported that its forces had downed and captured an MQM-170 US drone over Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate US military response to that claim, which Reuters could not independently verify.
Tehran also said it had destroyed an unmanned US vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
However, the US military's Central Command rejected the claim, saying all American unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East were accounted for, including a squadron of advanced sea drones patrolling the waterway.
The latest maritime incidents come amid heightened tensions following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February and subsequent Iranian attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure across the region.
Reuters reported earlier this month that Iran had shifted towards intensifying attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to keep oil prices elevated and increase pressure on Washington.
At least seven incidents involving tankers were reported during a week in early October, according to maritime intelligence service Marisks. The incidents included attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, raising concerns over the security of energy exports from the Gulf.
The maritime security crisis has coincided with a renewed Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia, further widening the conflict's geographical reach.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked several Saudi energy facilities, including the Ras Tanura refinery, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility at Abqaiq owned by state oil giant Saudi Aramco.
A Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region.
The attacks followed repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, oil installations and other critical infrastructure this month, including an October 10 attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Reuters.
The Houthis have also threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, warning civilians, workers and international shipping companies to stay away from sites they consider legitimate targets.
The renewed offensive has severely disrupted Saudi aviation. According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, 4,071 of 4,736 scheduled flights at Riyadh's airport, or 86%, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25.
More than 7,800 flights, accounting for 45% of scheduled departures across Saudi airports, were cancelled during the same period.
The United States on Friday confirmed that it had ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia, effective October 23, citing security risks from Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure.
The US embassy in Riyadh warned American citizens of possible further attacks, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.
The fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has intensified in recent weeks, opening another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
A truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition collapsed in July. The group subsequently declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, attacked Saudi vessels and the East-West pipeline, and seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Reuters.
The military escalation has continued despite diplomatic efforts involving regional powers to prevent the conflict from spreading further.
Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of coordinated efforts to reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country obtain medical supplies, following reports that Vance had written to Tehran's top security official in an effort to revive peace negotiations.
Iran has confirmed receiving Vance's letter but has yet to respond, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. Tehran has said Washington must meet its conditions for an agreement.
Earlier this week, Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials met Iranian leaders in Tehran and agreed to continue discussions, although the agenda and substance of the talks have not been disclosed.
Pakistan's military said on Friday it was "cautiously optimistic" about Islamabad's mediation efforts, following two visits to Tehran this month by Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin accompanied Munir during his latest visit.
The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7, under which an attack on any signatory is to be treated as an attack on all.
Pakistan's military spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said the agreement did not rule out additional members, including Iran, although any expansion would require a decision by the signatories' political leadership.
The mounting security risks have added to concerns over global energy supplies, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a critical chokepoint for crude oil and fuel shipments.
Oil prices rose more than 2% on Friday, settling at their highest levels since late April as traders weighed the possibility of further escalation and the risks to supplies from the Middle East.
Brent crude futures for December delivery settled $2.76 higher, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose $2.12, or 2.08%, to $104.12.
For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI rose 15.2%.
The attacks have raised concerns about the ability of Gulf producers to maintain exports through both the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, particularly as Saudi Arabia faces renewed threats to its oil infrastructure and Red Sea shipping access.
Saudi crude exports nevertheless increased in October compared with September, according to two of three ship-tracking companies cited by Reuters, despite Iranian attacks on shipping and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi energy facilities.
With Washington and Tehran yet to reach an agreement, the combination of maritime attacks, renewed fighting in Yemen and threats to Gulf energy infrastructure continues to complicate diplomatic efforts to contain the eight-month-old conflict.

high_priority_articles.title: UK CBAM records: why net mass, not CMR weight, matters - Trans.INFO
high_priority_articles.summary: UK CBAM records: why net mass, not CMR weight, matters  Trans.INFO
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Key points:
- UK CBAM applies to imports of aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, and iron and steel from 1 January 2027.
- Importers of £50,000 or more of CBAM goods in 12 months will be liable.
- For each import, they must record net mass in kilograms, excluding packaging, to up to 6 decimal places.
- Forwarders, hauliers and customs brokers do not become the importer by acting on the importer’s behalf.
- Importers that do not keep records may face a £500 fixed penalty.
Who pays
UK CBAM puts a carbon price on imports of five sectors: aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, and iron and steel. The aim is for imported goods to face a carbon cost comparable to that paid by UK producers.
The tax is paid by the importer. According to HMRC, this is the person named on the import declaration, even if someone else declares the goods for them. HMRC lists freight forwarders, hauliers (drivers), customs brokers, express operators and fast parcel operators among those who may import goods on someone else’s behalf. In all these cases, the business it is acting for “will still be classed as the importer”.
A business is liable once its CBAM imports reach £50,000 in 12 months, or if it expects to reach that amount within the next 30 days, according to the registration rules.
Gross weight is not enough
This is where transport companies come in. Under HMRC’s record-keeping guidance, importers must keep the following for every CBAM import from 1 January 2027:
- the 8-digit commodity code and a description of the goods,
- net mass in kilograms, excluding packaging, to up to 6 decimal places,
- the value of the goods,
- the date the goods entered the UK or cleared customs,
- proof of origin and evidence of any exemptions.
The records must be kept for 6 years. HMRC lists import declarations, bills of lading, commercial invoices, packing lists and “carrier weight records” among the documents that can support them.
In practice, a CMR or delivery note usually shows gross weight, including pallets and packaging. To get the net figure, importers will need packing lists or data from manufacturers. HMRC notes that weight evidence “might be from manufacturers”.
No border stop, but more data requests
CBAM is not collected at the border. Importers will register from 1 January 2028 and submit their first return and payment by 31 May 2028, covering imports from 2027.
However, importers will need the data from the very first shipment in January. Those who cannot obtain verified actual emissions data must use default values, and failing to keep records may lead to a fixed penalty of £500.
For forwarders and hauliers handling steel, aluminium or fertiliser loads into the UK, this means more requests for accurate documents. Customers may ask for packing lists, net weights and weighbridge records with each consignment, so it pays to agree in advance who provides which data.
For more on the basics, see our guides on who pays UK CBAM and on the HMRC rulebook published earlier this month.

high_priority_articles.title: Steel: Confimi’s Italian foundries take on Brussels – tariffs and the CBAM are hurting the supply chain - Eunews
high_priority_articles.summary: Steel: Confimi’s Italian foundries take on Brussels – tariffs and the CBAM are hurting the supply chain  Eunews
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Brussels – “Four months after the new European regime on steel imports came into force, almost 30 per cent of companies in the foundry and engineering sectors have seen a fall in orders due to rules that make it cheaper to buy semi-finished products from outside the EU.” This is how Flavio Lorenzin, president of Confimi Industria Meccanica, summarises in a statement the critical issues that emerged during the conference organised yesterday in Padua by the trade association together with Confimi Industria Veneto and Confimi Industria Padova-Rovigo. The companies present described difficulties that are jeopardising the continuity of production and fuelling mistrust towards the decisions taken in Brussels.
At the heart of the criticism lies an asymmetry in the trade defence system. “The EU imposes duties on imports of metallic materials when they enter as raw materials, but applies them at a negligible rate – or virtually none at all – when metal products are imported as semi-finished goods. The metal is the same; it is who pays that changes: companies that buy it as a raw material bear the cost, while those that import it in a processed form do not,” explains Lorenzin.
From 1 July 2026, the European regulation provides for a 50 per cent duty on steel imports exceeding the annual quotas, compared with 25 per cent under the previous safeguard measure. Furthermore, from 1 January, with the final phase of the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism), imports of cast iron, steel, and aluminium will also be subject to a charge linked to carbon dioxide emissions. Melted metals and many processed components from third countries, however, remain exempt from both mechanisms: the Commission has proposed extending the CBAM to over 400 downstream products from 2028, but the text is still under negotiation.
Meanwhile, prices are soaring. “From November 2025 to the present day, costs have risen by an average of 13 per cent for carbon steels, 16 per cent for stainless steels and 37 per cent for aluminium,” the chairman explains.
“Defending ‘Made in Italy’ is a political choice: if production costs in Europe are not reduced, businesses will either close or relocate,” warns Lorenzin. “We need lower taxes, less bureaucracy, competitively priced energy, flexible regulations, and a reduced tax wedge. And the cost of imports must be brought into line with the costs borne by European businesses.”
The association is therefore calling on Brussels to review import duties and to include semi-finished products, castings, and components in the CBAM negotiations; these are currently virtually duty-free and excluded from the mechanism. This measure is described as urgent but temporary, pending the introduction of an EU policy that restores competitiveness to Italian and European businesses without them having to rely on tariff protection.

Azerbaijani Presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev has discussed the peace process with Armenia during a conversation with American economist and professor Jeffrey Sachs in Baku.
Hajiyev spoke about bilateral trade relations, the development of transport links, and opportunities for cooperation in renewable energy.
He said Baku also views the peace process in the context of transforming the South Caucasus into a platform for cooperation.
“In our bilateral relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan, we are also putting the historical past aside. There are still unhealed wounds and memories that we cannot turn a blind eye to. At the same time, however, we are looking toward the future, toward lasting peace. Trade relations between the two countries have already begun. According to him, the country plans to have an additional 2 gigawatts of capacity in the coming years, followed by an additional 8 gigawatts of capacity ready for export.
Hajiyev said Baku also views these plans in the context of peacebuilding with Armenia.
“Now the war is over, and we are trying to present the economic benefits of the concept of peace, as well as the concept of green energy – the peace dividend. We hope that green energy will become one of the components of this strategy, including along the Caspian Sea,” he said.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.
Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.
Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.
“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.
September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.
“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.
The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.
“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.
Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.
The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.
By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.
“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

high_priority_articles.title: India must link industrial support to export competitiveness amid global supply shocks: CEA Nageswaran - ET Manufacturing
high_priority_articles.summary: India must link industrial support to export competitiveness amid global supply shocks: CEA Nageswaran  ET Manufacturing
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran on Thursday called for a shift in India's industrial strategy, saying support for domestic manufacturing must be linked to export competitiveness and the ability to match import prices, as global supply disruptions make access to critical resources increasingly uncertain.
Speaking at the ISID-IDRA Fourth National Conference during the inaugural session, Nageswaran said the country could no longer rely on markets to provide essential goods as smoothly as during the decades before the pandemic.
He said governments and industries must focus on building domestic capabilities and reducing dependence on supplies that could be restricted during geopolitical tensions.
Nageswaran said India's approach to import substitution must differ from earlier strategies and require industries to demonstrate stronger competitiveness. "So in other words, we have to insist on quid pro quo from the industry in terms of export competitiveness, and or import parity," he said.
He also cautioned that protection without investment to improve productivity could weaken industrial resilience. The presentation accompanying his remarks called for time-bound support linked to performance and exports, with protection withdrawn once domestic capacity becomes competitive.
The remarks come as India records strong economic and manufacturing growth amid global uncertainty. He cited real GDP growth of 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of 2026-27, manufacturing gross value added growth of 9.2 per cent and gross fixed capital formation growth of 11.9 per cent.
However, manufacturing's share of gross value added remained broadly unchanged at 14.8 per cent in 2025-26, compared with 14.7 per cent in 2022-23. The presentation also showed that core merchandise imports rose 19.7 per cent year-on-year during April-September 2026, faster than the 16.2 per cent growth in core exports.
"Last six years have seen many shocks with one common element - supply side shocks; semiconductor chip shortages, tariffs linked trade retaliation, vulnerability to crude oil", Nageswaran said.
He further added that conventional monetary and fiscal responses were less effective when the problem was a shortage of goods rather than weak demand.
"Monetary policy will be much more difficult to implement in a world of supply shocks," he said, adding that fiscal support would be more effective when directed towards production and productivity.
He also stressed the need to build buffers of essential commodities and strengthen domestic manufacturing so India can withstand external disruptions and become a more important supplier to global markets. (ANI)

He said the pact would add A$10 billion to the economy, expanding market access for beef, wine, minerals and services
Thursday, October 29, 2026
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used a press conference at Parliament House on Thursday, October 29, to press lawmakers to back legislation needed to put Australia’s trade agreement with the European Union into effect, arguing that the deal would widen market access for exporters at a time of rising global pressure on free trade.
Albanese said the agreement would make 98% of Australian exports of goods and services tariff-free in the EU, which he described as a market of 450 million people, and would add A$10 billion to the Australian economy. He said the gains would extend across critical minerals, services, manufacturing, fruit and vegetables, and wine, and would also increase access for beef and sheep meat exports.
“This is a good deal for Australia,” Albanese said, adding that failure to pass it would leave Australia at a disadvantage against countries that already have trade arrangements with the bloc, including New Zealand. He said that if Australia “shut ourselves out of this,” competing exporters would gain a comparative advantage in Europe.
The European agreement has become a political issue in Canberra as the government seeks parliamentary support for a wider economic agenda. Albanese said the deal was “front and centre” for the government even though the enabling measures were not being voted on during the final days of this week’s parliamentary sitting. He urged lawmakers to treat the agreement as a national economic priority.
According to Albanese, Coalition critics have argued that the agreement is a poor deal and objected to its climate language. He rejected both points, saying the government had previously walked away from an earlier version, returned to negotiations, and secured better terms. He also said references to the Paris climate agreement were not unusual, noting that climate provisions also appear in trade agreements with the United Kingdom, the United States, and China.
Albanese said the agreement would expand current access for red meat exporters, stating that sheep meat and beef quotas would rise to four and eight times current export levels, respectively, with a review after five years and the possibility of further increases. He also pointed to the government’s handling of geographical naming issues, citing feta as an example of a concern that had been addressed.
The issue matters beyond agriculture and heavy industry. If the agreement is implemented, it could improve Australian wine producers’ access to Europe while also opening the Australian market further to European products. That has the potential to alter competition and pricing across parts of the beverage sector, especially for wine, even as the exact commercial effects would depend on how producers and importers respond.
Albanese said cheaper imports under the agreement would help put downward pressure on prices for Australian consumers. He framed that argument within a broader defense of trade liberalization, saying Australia should present itself in global forums as a country that supports “free and fair trade unequivocally.”
His push on the EU deal came alongside other major items on the government’s parliamentary agenda. Albanese said the House of Representatives had passed the government’s Digital Duty of Care legislation on Wednesday, October 28, and called on the Senate to approve it. He said the bill would make large technology companies more accountable for content carried on their platforms and give users greater control over the material they receive through algorithms.
He also said tax legislation would be taken up on Thursday, October 29, describing it as part of a broader effort to align taxation of labor income and asset income more closely. Albanese acknowledged that tax reform is difficult and said the government had already adjusted measures through consultation, but he maintained that the overall approach was necessary to avoid placing more of the tax burden on wage earners.
Another major vote on Thursday, October 29, concerned the government’s domestic gas reservation package. Standing with Resources Minister Madeleine King, Industry Minister Tim Ayres, and Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, Albanese said the bill would allow the government to reserve up to 20% of gas exports for domestic use. He said that would increase supply for Australian manufacturers and help reduce domestic prices.
King called the package a “landmark” reform and said it would create a long-term framework for households, businesses, manufacturers, and the gas industry. Ayres said the measure went directly to Australia’s industrial competitiveness and would help secure heavy industrial jobs in outer suburbs and regional areas. Bowen said Australia was unusual among major gas-producing countries in not having an effective reservation policy and said the legislation would change that.
The government’s trade and energy messages were closely tied to cost-of-living concerns that dominated several questions at the press conference. Albanese said households were still facing pressure from inflation and the risk of further interest-rate increases, and he argued that the government’s strategy combined budget restraint with targeted measures such as free technical education, cheaper medicines, and health spending.
He said global factors remained central to the inflation outlook, pointing to higher oil prices and conflict in the Middle East. Those pressures, he said, were feeding through not only into fuel costs but also into the price of goods transported across the economy.
Albanese also used the appearance to place the trade push in a broader international context. He said he would attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in November and would use overseas meetings to advance Australia’s economic and diplomatic priorities, including trade and its campaign for a United Nations Security Council seat.
When asked about criticism from within the opposition’s ranks, Albanese said it was surprising that support for freer trade was being questioned in a party that has long presented itself as market-oriented. He warned that resistance to the EU agreement would move Australian politics toward protectionism at a moment when trade barriers are becoming a larger issue internationally.
Albanese said the debate was especially important because the global trade environment has become more uncertain. He argued that Australia’s growth and productivity depend on international engagement and said the EU agreement should be seen in the same context as the government’s earlier trade efforts with the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, and Southeast Asia.

high_priority_articles.title: Peru's updated trade deal with China is now in force, but it does not deliver broad new tariff cuts - Latin Times
high_priority_articles.summary: Peru's updated trade deal with China is now in force, but it does not deliver broad new tariff cuts  Latin Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Peru's Optimization Protocol for its Free Trade Agreement with China entered into force on November 1, 2026, reshaping a 16-year-old pact across digital commerce, customs procedures, agricultural access, supply chains, and investment rules. The revamped deal governs a bilateral corridor that generated $32.6 billion in Peruvian exports to China in 2025 — a 30.1% increase over 2024 and approximately 140% above what the corridor moved in 2019.
The timing is not accidental. The update arrives as new U.S. tariff pressures weigh on certain Peruvian export flows, pushing Lima toward a structural deepening of its most critical trade partnership — one that now accounts for 35% of Peru's total commercial exchange, according to the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism.
The 12-Chapter Upgrade, Broken Down
Five chapters in the protocol cover entirely new ground that the 2010 agreement never touched: standards and compliance assessment, competition policy, e-commerce, global supply chains, and environmental trade commitments. The seven revised chapters address rules of origin, customs procedures, sanitary and phytosanitary standards, intellectual property, services, temporary business entry, and investment.
Among the most commercially consequential changes are the updated rules of origin, which determine whether a product qualifies as Peruvian or Chinese for preferential tariff access — a technical but downstream-decisive update. The new supply chain chapter creates a cooperation and data-sharing framework around transport documentation and logistics performance metrics, according to the full protocol text published by Mincetur.
The $32.6 Billion Relationship — and Who Dominates It
Mining accounts for more than 90% of what Peru sends to China, with copper concentrates leading the mix — followed by gold, silver, and lead. Through the first eight months of 2026, Peru dispatched $28.3 billion in goods to China, a 39% year-on-year increase, as the bilateral corridor extended its record-setting streak.
In the first quarter of 2026 alone, Peruvian exports to China reached $10.748 billion, growing 42.6% against the same period in 2025, while Chinese imports into Peru climbed to $5.003 billion, up 19.4%, driven by automotive and heavy industry goods.
Which Sectors Stand to Gain
While mining will continue to dominate the relationship, the optimization was specifically engineered to open pathways for sectors left largely on the sidelines by the original deal. Trade Minister Rogers Valencia pointed to agriculture and fishing as clear beneficiaries, given Peru's climatic versatility and China's growing appetite for imported produce. The copper manufacturing segment — including processed wire and tubing products with higher added value — was also flagged as having significant untapped potential in the Chinese market, alongside information technology, wood, and paper products, according to Gestión's reporting on Valencia's remarks.
Former Trade Minister Mercedes Araoz, who led the original FTA negotiations as commerce minister from 2006 to 2009, welcomed the upgrade as overdue, citing what she called low utilization of the trade framework during its first decade. Her comments reflected a view widely shared among Peruvian trade economists that the 2010 agreement delivered far less than its agricultural and value-added export potential warranted.
The SME Angle: Smaller Companies, Lower Friction
The new customs cooperation provisions were drafted with micro, small, and medium enterprises specifically in mind. The framework enables direct recognition of certificates of origin between the two countries' customs authorities, cutting compliance costs and accelerating clearance times for exporters who historically bore the heaviest administrative burden when invoking FTA preferences. Mincetur confirmed that the modernization was designed to serve companies now operating in a global trade environment fundamentally different from the one that existed when the FTA first came into force.
The Critical Caveat: No Tariff Windfall
The optimization protocol does not unlock across-the-board preferential tariff cuts. Exporters who anticipated broad duty reductions as of November 1 will need to recalibrate: what the deal actually delivers is better-defined rules, cleaner procedures, and a new legal architecture for digital transactions and environmental commitments — not cheaper border access in blanket terms. Real economic impact will depend heavily on implementation quality and corporate uptake on both sides of the Pacific, the Peruvian-Chinese Chamber of Commerce noted in announcing the deal's entry into force.
Strategic Context: APEC Shenzhen and the U.S. Factor
Peru's trade ministry has framed the protocol's November 1 activation as strategically timed ahead of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, scheduled for November 18–19, 2026, where Lima intends to present itself as a logistics and services hub for the broader Latin American market.
The original Peru-China FTA was signed in Beijing on April 28, 2009, and entered into force on March 1, 2010. The optimization protocol was signed on November 14, 2024, during Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Lima for the APEC summit, formally ratified on July 25, 2026, and now goes live with all required diplomatic notifications confirmed as complete.

high_priority_articles.summary: France and Germany move to exclude Moroccan-made cars from EU manufacturing incentives  HESPRESS English - Morocco News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
France and Germany have reached an agreement that could exclude cars manufactured in Morocco from preferential European Union subsidies and public procurement programs, potentially disadvantaging Renault and Stellantis factories that supply the European market, according to European automotive industry reporting and an analysis by the Jacques Delors Institute.
The agreement, announced on October 16, would favour vehicles produced within the EU and certain European partner countries, leaving Morocco and Turkey outside the proposed definition of “Made in Europe.”
The distinction matters because the proposed rules could determine which manufacturers benefit from public financial support as Europe seeks to strengthen its automotive industry against growing Chinese competition. They would not prohibit Moroccan-made vehicles from entering the EU market.
The Franco-German compromise links two previously contested issues: European manufacturing preferences and the bloc’s 2035 emissions requirements for new cars.
Germany secured French support for relaxing the proposed emissions target to a 90% reduction, while France obtained German backing for a narrower definition of European production, according to Agence Europe.
The agreement is intended to influence negotiations over the Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed by the European Commission in March.
The legislation would introduce European-content and low-carbon requirements into selected public procurement contracts and subsidy programmes, including those covering vehicles, steel and clean technologies.
Morocco’s potential exclusion has raised questions about its place in European automotive supply chains.
Renault operates major factories in Tangier and Casablanca, while Stellantis manufactures vehicles in Kenitra. Their production networks link Moroccan facilities with European manufacturers and suppliers.
Guillaume Duval, an adviser to the Jacques Delors Institute, criticized the compromise in an October 27 analysis, arguing that excluding Morocco and Turkey could undermine Europe’s efforts to develop competitive production networks closer to home.
Duval said European manufacturers need lower-cost neighbouring production bases to compete with Chinese companies, particularly in markets outside Europe.
The exclusion could also conflict with the EU’s stated objective of strengthening economic integration with Mediterranean partners, he argued.

high_priority_articles.title: Why Southeast Asia has attracted strong FDI inflows, from advanced manufacturing to the digital economy - Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
high_priority_articles.summary: Why Southeast Asia has attracted strong FDI inflows, from advanced manufacturing to the digital economy  Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Uncertainty has become the new normal for global businesses, with a mix of geopolitical tensions and macroeconomic concerns forcing them to prioritise resilience and restructure supply chains. This has impacted global Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), which fell by 11 per cent in 2024, following a 10 per cent drop in 2023, according to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025.
Against this backdrop, Southeast Asia has defied the odds and emerged as the bright spot for growth, with foreign direct investment (FDI) growing year on year. In 2024, Southeast Asia accounted for 15 per cent of global FDI inflows, attracting US$226 billion, a rise of 8 per cent from 2023. Since 2021, annual FDI inflows have consistently exceeded US$200 billion, above the previous decade’s annual average of under US$130 billion.
In fact, FDI stock in ASEAN rose from US$1 trillion in 2010 to US$3.6 trillion in 2024, equivalent to 1.2 times the combined stock in Africa and South America. Here are five highlights from the report that explain why MNCs are doubling down on Southeast Asia and why Singapore is their strategic hub for expansion.
1. More greenfield investments across diverse manufacturing sectors
Investments into Southeast Asia are increasingly driven by new and expansionary projects. More than two-thirds of inflows comprise of equity capital, while cross-border mergers and acquisitions fell by 61 per cent from 2023.
This signals that businesses are not simply acquiring firms or restructuring their balance sheets. Instead, they are establishing new operations, expanding production capacity, and building long-term capabilities across the region.
Furthermore, manufacturing FDI rose sharply, increasing by 147 per cent year-on-year, particularly in supply chain-intensive sectors such as automotive, electronics and semiconductors. Many of these big-ticket investments were either first-time entries into Southeast Asia or involved significant upgrading and expansion of existing facilities. These investments were driven by rising regional demand and the adoption of advanced manufacturing technologies to improve efficiency and resilience.
Investment spanned major economies, with Chinese firms active in automotive and apparel, US firms in pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, UK investors in aerospace and energy, and other Asian multinationals across automotive and electronics.
2. Digital economy investment is accelerating
Alongside manufacturing growth, investment in Southeast Asia’s digital economy is rising rapidly. Greenfield investment in digital-related sectors more than doubled to US$16 billion in 2024, reflecting rising demand and growing investor confidence in the region’s digital infrastructure, connectivity, and technology ecosystem.
This growth was driven by expansion in data centres, cloud services, software development and technology-enabled business activities. These investments are critical as they strengthen the region’s digital backbone – supporting advanced manufacturing, supply chain coordination, digital trade and cross-border services.
Some of these investments in Singapore include Amazon’s AWS APAC Hub, OpenAI’s APAC Hub, and Databrick’s Asia Pacific & Japan Hub.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a key digital technology across Southeast Asia, with companies adopting AI to enhance their supply chains by optimising logistics and improving inventory management. Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand are leading the region in industrial robot installations, with Singapore ranking second globally in robot density, with 730 robots per 10,000 employees in 2023 – significantly above the global average of 162.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged has offered some support to Indian equities, but the relief may prove short-lived if domestic interest rates rise in the coming months.
Sensex jumped 762 points or 1% to the day's high of 74,007.70, while the broader Nifty 50 rose 210 points or 0.9% to an intra-day high of 22,908.75.
Emkay expects the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to deliver another 75 basis points of cumulative rate hikes in the current cycle, with increases anticipated in December 2026 and February 2027. This raises a key question for investors: can the Nifty sustain its gains amid the prospect of tighter domestic monetary policy, elevated crude oil prices and persistent inflationary pressures?
The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to maintain the US federal funds target range at 3.75%-4%, following a rate hike at its September meeting. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation remained too high and indicated that policymakers needed more data before deciding on their next move. US consumer inflation stood at 3.7% in September.
Domestic brokerage Emkay believes the combination of elevated US interest rates, high oil prices and weak natural dollar inflows could push the RBI towards further monetary tightening. These factors could increase pressure on the rupee and raise India's risk premium, limiting the central bank's ability to look through global inflationary pressures.
The brokerage expects 75 basis points of cumulative rate hikes in the current cycle, including 25-basis-point increases in December 2026 and February 2027. Its assessment is based on the view that resilient domestic growth gives the RBI room to respond to inflation risks, while policymakers are likely to favour measured rather than aggressive tightening.
For equity investors, the prospect of higher interest rates could weigh on valuations, particularly in expensive market segments. Higher borrowing costs may also affect companies with significant debt or those whose earnings depend on strong consumer demand.
The Fed's decision to hold rates steady could provide temporary relief to emerging markets by reducing immediate concerns about further US monetary tightening. However, the outlook for Indian equities will also depend on the trajectory of US bond yields, the dollar, crude oil prices and foreign portfolio investment flows.
Ajitabh Bharti, co-founder and executive director of Capital XB, viewed the Fed's decision as supportive for India in the near term because a softer US policy stance could ease pressure on the rupee and stabilise capital flows. However, he questioned whether the decision adequately addressed persistent inflation risks.
"The Fed's latest decision has come across as notably dovish — and somewhat surprising, given that inflation continues to run well above target. Easing the policy stance at this stage carries a genuine risk that the central bank could lose control of price pressures just when credibility matters most," Bharti said.
He also warned that perceptions of political influence over monetary policy could undermine confidence in the dollar, creating uncertainty for global markets.
Thomas Priju, portfolio manager at Karma Capital, warned that rising US rates could create volatility in Indian equities by keeping bond yields and the dollar elevated. He also highlighted the vulnerability of high-valuation stocks and companies dependent on foreign portfolio flows.
“For Indian equities, the implications could be significant. A further increase in US interest rates could keep US bond yields and the dollar elevated, putting pressure on emerging-market capital flows and increasing volatility in the Nifty. High-valuation stocks and segments dependent on foreign portfolio flows could remain particularly sensitive to changes in global liquidity conditions,” said the brokerage.
Priju said investors should focus on businesses with strong earnings visibility and healthy balance sheets while monitoring US inflation data and the Fed's subsequent communication for clues about the interest-rate outlook.
“However, the impact on Indian markets will also depend on domestic earnings growth, valuations and the trajectory of foreign investor flows. Investors should remain selective and focus on companies with strong earnings visibility and balance sheets, while monitoring US inflation data and the Fed’s subsequent communication for clues on the future rate trajectory,” he added.
His assessment suggests that the Fed's rate decision alone may not be sufficient to sustain a market rally. Domestic earnings performance, valuations and foreign investor activity will remain important determinants of the Nifty's direction.
