The market widely expects the Bank of Japan to hold its benchmark interest rate steady on Friday, while signaling that underlying inflation has finally reached its 2% target. A key question is whether the central bank will announce that, for the first time since setting the target in 2013, core inflation has broadly hit the 2% goal—a development that appears highly likely.
Zhitong Finance APP has learned that economists generally expect the Bank of Japan to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Friday, while noting that underlying inflation has finally reached and remained above its 2% target for an extended period. This milestone will strengthen the case for further rate hikes.
In a recent Bloomberg survey of economists worldwide, all respondents who have long monitored the Bank of Japan's policy trajectory expect the central bank to hold its policy rate steady at the conclusion of its two-day meeting this week. Last month, the Bank of Japan raised its key interest rate to 1.25%.
As shown in the chart above, the Bank of Japan under Kazuo Ueda is still steadily advancing its interest-rate hike process.
A key focus on Friday will be whether the Bank of Japan signals that underlying inflation has broadly reached its 2% target. This would be the first time since the target was set in 2013, and such an outcome appears quite likely. It would bolster the case for further interest-rate hikes, as Japan's borrowing costs remain relatively low and continue to provide a stimulus.
Ryutaro Kawano, Chief Economist for Japan at BNP Paribas, stated: "The Bank of Japan likely judges that underlying inflation has now reached around 2%. The central bank may believe it is necessary to raise interest rates to a neutral level as soon as reasonably feasible, but the upside risks to inflation are not yet sufficient to compel it to hike rates at two consecutive meetings."
Ahead of the Bank of Japan's meeting, the Federal Reserve left its policy settings unchanged overnight. The decision weighed on the U.S. dollar, pushing the yen to around 157.84 per dollar in Tokyo on Thursday morning.
Although the Bank of Japan has remained relatively vague about the true level of underlying inflation, numerous indicators have long suggested that inflation is taking root in Japan. In March this year, the Bank began publishing a new set of price measures designed to track changes in core inflation after stripping out factors that are largely temporary.
Raising the baseline inflation forecast will lay the groundwork for another interest-rate hike at the December meeting. More than 80% of surveyed economists expect the central bank to act then. In September, the Bank of Japan adjusted its policy rate, marking the second rate increase in three months and signaling the fastest pace of tightening in 36 years.
Sources told Bloomberg earlier this month that, given current price trends and the central bank's assessment that interest-rate hikes to date have had only limited impact on the economy, the Bank of Japan may continue raising rates at roughly the same pace.
Kazuo Ueda has increasingly stated that core inflation is "very close" to 2%, seemingly preparing investors for a shift in wording in Friday's quarterly outlook report. Earlier this month, he indicated that the Bank of Japan would not allow core inflation to rise significantly further from its current level.
Acknowledging that underlying inflation has already reached its target will prompt the market to focus more on how much further interest rates need to rise before policy ceases to be stimulative. The Bank of Japan estimates that the neutral rate lies between 1.1% and 2.5%, while emphasizing that it is difficult to determine precisely. Institutions such as JPMorgan Securities and BNP Paribas expect the terminal rate in this cycle to reach 2.5%.
The inflation gauge that excludes fresh food has long been a key metric of focus for the Bank of Japan. As of March this year, it has exceeded the central bank's target for four consecutive fiscal years; if the bank's latest projections prove accurate, it will have remained above target for six straight years. Some economists argue that the Bank of Japan has been overly cautious in acknowledging this shift, risking falling behind the curve in addressing inflation.
The above chart indicates that Japan's inflation is expected to remain above the Bank of Japan's 2% target. Note: All figures are annualized.
Kameida, a former economist at the Bank of Japan and currently an executive economist at Sompo Institute Plus, stated: "Five to six years is generally enough time for a first-grader to advance to junior high school. If someone were to claim that inflation persisting over this entire period still does not constitute a trend, it would be hard to imagine anyone accepting such a view."
Recent economic data, along with early signals ahead of next year's wage negotiations, indicate that inflationary pressures remain firm. Last month, a key measure of core inflation in Japan surged to 3.2%, the highest level in three years. Following three consecutive years of record‑high wage growth, Japan's largest trade union federation plans to seek even larger pay increases in the upcoming round of talks, which are expected to conclude with an agreement in March.
Taro Kimura, an economist at Bloomberg Economics, said: "Ahead of next year's annual wage negotiations, early signals from both labor and management leaders suggest that Japan's wage growth could accelerate in 2027. This could further fuel inflation and increase the risk that the Bank of Japan will raise its benchmark interest rate above the roughly 2% terminal level currently priced into the market."
The divergence among the Bank of Japan's nine policy board members over the inflation outlook was already reflected in last month's 7‑to‑2 vote. That outcome left the yen weaker even after the rate hike. Investors will be watching Friday's vote for signs of further momentum behind rate increases.
Reaching this milestone in the price‑level target would mark the culmination of a policy effort that began in 2013, when the Bank of Japan launched a massive monetary easing program aimed at achieving 2% inflation within roughly two years. However, Japan did not experience sustained price increases until nearly a decade later—driven in part by the global inflationary shock triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
In March 2024, as the Bank of Japan grew increasingly confident that its core inflation target was on track to be achieved, it ended the world's last negative interest rate policy and its yield curve control program. Kazuo Ueda has raised interest rates six times to date, marking the highest number of rate hikes by a single Bank of Japan governor in at least half a century.
In a recent podcast episode, former Deputy Governor Hiroshi Nakaso, who spent nearly four decades at the Bank of Japan, underscored this long-awaited economic shift. Prior to this, following the bursting of the asset bubble in the 1990s, Japan endured "the Lost Three Decades," during which roughly 200 financial institutions collapsed.
"Japan is back," said Hiroshi Nakaso. "Deflation has finally become a thing of the past, and the economy is shifting toward an inflationary regime."
However, achieving the target does not signify an unqualified success for inflation. While price increases have been accompanied by record corporate profits, nominal GDP, and tax revenues, they have also heightened concerns about the cost of living, particularly among Japan's rapidly aging population. Nearly 30 percent of Japanese citizens are aged 65 or older, and roughly 40 percent of elderly households rely entirely on pensions for their income.
Hiroshi Nakaso once stated that he would pop open a bottle of champagne to celebrate when the central bank achieves its price stability target. He emphasized that even after the Bank of Japan meets its goal, the government will still need to formulate a robust growth strategy.
Zhong Zenghong said, "This necessity has not diminished in the slightest."
The Bank of Japan's "hawkish pause" is imminent: the 2% inflation milestone continues to pave the way for the next steps in its rate-hike trajectory.
The most significant potential change at this Bank of Japan meeting is the first explicit acknowledgment that underlying inflation has broadly reached the 2% target, while maintaining the policy rate at 1.25%, thereby strengthening the rationale for continuing the exit from accommodative monetary policy.
Here, "underlying inflation" refers to the central bank's assessment of the persistent price trend after stripping out temporary factors; it is not equivalent to the consumer price index for any given month. Japan's inflation measure excluding fresh food has remained above 2% for several years, yet the central bank has continued to await stronger, sustained evidence from wage growth, service prices, and firms' pricing behavior. In a Bloomberg survey, all surveyed analysts expect a pause this week, while more than 80% of the economists polled anticipate a rate hike in December. Early signals from wage negotiations suggest that wage increases in 2027 could further reinforce inflationary stickiness. While maintaining its benchmark rate, the central bank also indicated for the first time that underlying inflation has hit the 2% goal, a milestone that could pave the way for another rate hike as early as December.
Zhitong Finance APP learned that, as the market had anticipated, the Bank of Japan kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged during Friday's Asian midday session, following the monetary policy moves of the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. At the same time, in its official monetary policy statement, the Bank of Japan for the first time indicated that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target. Achieving the inflation target means that the Bank of Japan must now shift from boosting inflation to ensuring it does not exceed the target level. Given these upside risks to inflation, more than 80% of surveyed economists expect the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates again in December.

Following the Bank of Japan's Monetary Policy Committee vote of 8 to 1 to keep interest rates unchanged, the yen briefly strengthened by 0.4% to 157.12 per U.S. dollar. All 53 Japanese economists surveyed by Bloomberg had previously anticipated this decision.
This trend unfolded on Friday as global markets shifted toward safe-haven assets, with tech stocks falling and oil prices rising. The yen has begun to signal a return to its traditional role as a safe haven. For years, during periods of market stress, the wider interest-rate differential and Japan's substantial overseas investment flows had exerted a stronger influence on the currency than safe-haven demand.
As shown in the chart above, following the Bank of Japan's policy decision, the yen-dollar exchange rate quickly widened its gains, underscoring the pace of the yen's appreciation.
OCBC Bank's FX strategist, Moh Siong Sim, said that the central bank's confirmation that its official inflation target has been met "signals further policy tightening ahead" and "should provide support for the yen." However, "the risk of another escalation in U.S.-Iran tensions following the U.S. midterm elections has pushed oil prices higher, potentially preventing the yen from fully benefiting from the weaker dollar environment driven by AI-related concerns."
Goldman Sachs strategists previously stated that, as Japan's policy environment shifts and global yields rise, the risk of a sharp yen depreciation has diminished, making the yen a more effective hedge against market shocks triggered by AI.
Last week, a selloff in global tech stocks boosted demand for safe-haven assets, pushing the yen to a more than one-month high of 156.08 per U.S. dollar.
Meanwhile, long-term Japanese government bonds have been performing strongly recently, with signs of a rebound in domestic demand and a more favorable policy environment further boosting the appeal of their higher yields. The yield on 30-year JGBs has already fallen by roughly 40 basis points from this month's peak of 4.25%.
The Bank of Japan announced that, starting in January, it will increase the annual pace of ETF sales from roughly 330 billion yen to about 860 billion yen. Shogo Karitani, a strategist at a Hong Kong bank, said: "The ETF‑selling plan came as a surprise. It is being viewed as a strong hawkish move by the Bank of Japan, as it signals further progress in monetary policy normalization, thereby prompting some modest yen buying."
As the scale of AI‑related infrastructure development among global technology firms continues to surge, driving overall corporate growth to record highs this year, yield metrics in the global credit bond market have steadily deteriorated. Consequently, financing costs for Japanese companies—particularly those tied to AI—have risen markedly, and credit spreads across various segments have widened broadly.
Traders will be watching the press conference by Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda following the decision, which typically begins at 3:30 p.m. Tokyo time.
The Real Shift Behind the "Hawkish Pause": Official Inflation Assessments Have Crossed a Key Threshold, and ETF Liquidations Have Accelerated Unexpectedly

Following the release of the decision, the yen briefly widened its gains against the dollar to around 0.4%, reaching 157.12, while Nikkei futures extended their losses.
"Meeting the core inflation target" signals a shift in the Bank of Japan's assessment of the underlying price trend. In its official outlook, the bank revised up its forecast for the CPI excluding fresh food to 2.6% for fiscal year 2027, from 2.4%, while lowering its projection for real GDP growth over the same period to 0.7% from 0.8%, painting a picture of moderate growth amid still‑strong price pressures. The acceleration of ETF sell‑offs has reinforced the signal that unconventional monetary easing is being unwound. high_priority_articles.title: Glencore cobalt output sinks 52% under DRC quotas - Mining.com
high_priority_articles.summary: Glencore cobalt output sinks 52% under DRC quotas  Mining.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Glencore (LON: GLEN), one of the world’s largest cobalt producers, reported a 52% drop in output during the first nine months of 2026 as export quotas in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) prompted it to leave more of the battery metal unprocessed.
The Swiss-based miner produced 13,700 tonnes of its own-sourced cobalt through September, down from 28,500 tonnes a year earlier, according to its third-quarter production report released Thursday. Output fell 20% quarter-on-quarter to 3,500 tonnes.
Glencore said it is increasingly retaining cobalt contained in mixed ore in solution rather than converting it into saleable hydroxide, cutting near-term processing costs. The company expects to recover the metal’s value as export regulations evolve, but excludes the retained material from reported production.
The strategy illustrates how the DRC’s efforts to control cobalt supply are changing mining operations, with companies delaying processing rather than producing material they cannot immediately export. It also raises the prospect of additional supply entering the market once restrictions ease.
Cobalt restrictions
The DRC, the world’s dominant cobalt-producing country, suspended exports in 2025 after prices slumped to nine-year lows. Authorities subsequently introduced quotas aimed at supporting prices, with restrictions expected to remain in place until at least the end of 2027.
Glencore said its Kamoto Copper Company (KCC) and Mutanda operations hold enough cobalt stocks to meet near-term export allocations. Its African Copper division, which includes the Congolese mines, produced 11,600 tonnes of cobalt through September, down 56% year-on-year.
The volume of cobalt being held in solution remains undisclosed, making it difficult to assess how much additional supply could eventually reach the market.
Copper operations, meanwhile, delivered stronger results. Glencore’s own-sourced production rose 3% to 598,600 tonnes from 583,500 tonnes a year earlier. Excluding the closure of Mount Isa’s copper mine and the sale of Kidd, output increased 12% on a comparable basis.
Higher mining rates and improved grades at African Copper, together with richer ore at Peru’s Antamina mine, offset weaker production at Antapaccay and Collahuasi.
Glencore aims to produce 1.6 million tonnes of copper annually by 2035, nearly double its current level, as it pursues demand from electrification, power grids and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Production outlook
The company maintained its 2026 copper guidance of 810,000 to 870,000 tonnes, although it expects to finish near the bottom of that range. Steelmaking coal output is also tracking toward the lower end of its 30 million to 32 million-tonne target, while zinc and energy coal are expected near the upper ends of their forecasts.
“We are pleased to report a strong third quarter production performance, where our key assets largely performed in line with expectations and previously communicated guidance,” CEO Gary Nagle said.
BMO Capital Markets analyst Alexander Pearce said in a note the company’s quarterly production was slightly below expectations overall. Copper and steelmaking coal missed estimates by 3% and 7%, respectively, while zinc and thermal coal exceeded forecasts by 4% and 5%.
Pearce noted Glencore’s full-year outlook remained broadly consistent with BMO’s forecasts, indicating that the quarterly shortfalls could be offset during the final three months of 2026.
Steelmaking coal production declined 13% to 21.5 million tonnes through September because of lower plant throughput and yields at its EVR operations. Energy coal output edged up to 73.9 million tonnes from 73.5 million tonnes a year earlier.
Glencore also advanced the restart of its ferrochrome smelters, bringing Boshoek back online in September and Wonderkop in October, following the earlier restart of Lion. Attributable ferrochrome production climbed 29% from the second quarter.
The company reiterated its forecast for full-year marketing, adjusted earnings before interest and taxes to exceed $5 billion.

After the Cold War, NATO was reconceived as a “cooperative-security” organization whose mandate was to include two main objectives: to foster dialogue and cooperation with former adversaries in the Warsaw Pact and to “manage” conflicts in areas on the European periphery, such as the Balkans. In keeping with the first objective, NATO established the North Atlantic Cooperation Council (1991; later replaced by the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council) to provide a forum for the exchange of views on political and security issues, as well as the enhance European security and stability through joint military training exercises with NATO and non-NATO states, including the former Soviet republics and allies. Special cooperative links were also set up with two PfP countries: Russia and Ukraine.
NATO in the former Yugoslavia and expansion into eastern Europe
The second objective entailed NATO’s first use of military force, when it entered the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995 by staging air strikes against Bosnian Serb positions around the capital city of Sarajevo. The subsequent Dayton Accords, which were initialed by representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, committed each state to respecting the others’ sovereignty and to settling disputes peacefully; it also laid the groundwork for stationing NATO peacekeeping troops in the region. A 60,000-strong Implementation Force (IFOR) was initially deployed, though a smaller contingent remained in Bosnia under a different name, the Stabilization Force (SFOR). In March 1999 NATO launched massive air strikes against Serbia in an attempt to force the Yugoslav government of Slobodan Milošević to accede to diplomatic provisions designed to protect the predominantly Muslim Albanian population in the province of Kosovo. Under the terms of a negotiated settlement to the fighting, NATO deployed a peacekeeping force called the Kosovo Force (KFOR).
The crisis over Kosovo and the ensuing war gave renewed impetus to efforts by the European Union (EU) to construct a new crisis-intervention force, which would make the EU less dependent on NATO and U.S. military resources for conflict management. These efforts prompted significant debates about whether enhancing the EU’s defensive capabilities would strengthen or weaken NATO. Simultaneously there was much discussion of the future of NATO in the post-Cold War era. Some observers argued that the alliance should be dissolved, noting that it was created to confront an enemy that no longer existed; others called for a broad expansion of NATO membership to include Russia. Most suggested alternative roles, including peacekeeping. By the start of the second decade of the 21st century, it appeared likely that the EU would not develop capabilities competitive with those of NATO or even seek to do so; as a result, earlier worries associated with the spectre of rivalry between the two Brussels-based organizations dissipated.
During the presidency of Bill Clinton (1993–2001), the United States led an initiative to enlarge NATO membership gradually to include some of the former Soviet allies. In the concurrent debate over enlargement, supporters of the initiative argued that NATO membership was the best way to begin the long process of integrating these states into regional political and economic institutions such as the EU. Some also feared future Russian aggression and suggested that NATO membership would guarantee freedom and security for the newly democratic regimes. Opponents pointed to the enormous cost of modernizing the military forces of new members; they also argued that enlargement, which Russia would regard as a provocation, would hinder democracy in that country and enhance the influence of hard-liners. Despite these disagreements, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland joined NATO in 1999; Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia were admitted in 2004 (these former Soviet and Warsaw Pact states later formed an extraordinary group known as the Bucharest Nine as a response to Russian aggression in the region). Albania and Croatia acceded to the alliance in 2009.
NATO relations with Russia in the post-September 11 world
Meanwhile, by the beginning of the 21st century, Russia and NATO had formed a strategic relationship. No longer considered NATO’s chief enemy, Russia cemented a new cooperative bond with NATO in 2001 to address such common concerns as international terrorism, nuclear nonproliferation, and arms control. This bond subsequently frayed, however, due to regional aggression by Russian Pres. Vladimir Putin. After Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, NATO strengthened ties with the latter country and established the NATO-Georgia Commission “to help Georgia achieve its goal of membership in NATO.” In 2014 pro-Russian Ukrainian Pres. Viktor Yanukovych fled months of popular protests, and Russia responded by invading the Ukrainian autonomous republic of Crimea. Russia illegally annexed Crimea and fomented uprisings in Ukraine’s Donbas region in an effort to reassert control over its neighbour. Ukraine checked the Russian-backed campaign in the Donbas, and NATO reaffirmed its support for Ukraine’s democratically elected government and its internationally recognized borders.
Events following the September 11 attacks in 2001 led to the forging of a new dynamic within the alliance, one that increasingly favoured the military engagement of members outside Europe, initially with a mission against Taliban forces in Afghanistan beginning in the summer of 2003 and subsequently with air operations against the regime of Muammar al-Qaddafi in Libya in early 2011. As a result of the increased tempo of military operations undertaken by the alliance, the long-standing issue of “burden sharing” was revived, with some officials warning that failure to share the costs of NATO operations more equitably would lead to unraveling of the alliance. At the time, however, most observers regarded that scenario as unlikely.
Later, the burden-sharing issue was raised once more by U.S. Pres. Donald Trump, who repeatedly criticized other NATO members for failing to devote a sufficient portion of their budgets to defense spending. Trump questioned the relevance of NATO and discussed withdrawing the United States from the alliance; even the suggestion of such an action was seen as a boon to Putin. However, Trump’s national security team moved to reassure allies that the U.S. remained committed to NATO, and, by the end of Trump’s term in 2021, the U.S. troop presence in Europe was almost entirely unchanged.
NATO and the Russian invasion of Ukraine
By the end of 2021, Russia had begun a massive military buildup along the Ukrainian frontier under the guise of joint maneuvers with the Belarusian army. In February 2022 there were as many as 190,000 Russian troops along the Russo-Ukrainian border, in Belarus, in Russian-occupied Crimea, and in the Russian-backed separatist enclave of Transdniestria in Moldova. On February 24 Putin announced the beginning of a “special military operation” and launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Although the Russians made some early gains, their advances soon stalled against a spirited Ukrainian defense.
Ukrainian Pres. Volodymyr Zelensky appealed to Western countries for military aid, and individual NATO members began a massive transfer of hardware to bolster the Ukrainian arsenal. The administration of U.S. Pres. Joe Biden took a leading role in marshaling the response to the greatest threat to European security since World War II. The speed and unity of NATO’s reaction to Russian aggression in Ukraine dramatically dispelled any doubts about the continued relevance of the alliance.
Sweden and Finland, two countries with a long history of neutrality, announced their intention to join NATO in the wake of the Russian invasion, and the U.S. deployed additional military assets to Poland and the Baltic states. In June 2022, at the first annual NATO summit since the invasion, NATO Secretary-General Jens Stoltenberg announced “the biggest overhaul of our collectivedeterrence and defense since the Cold War.” In addition to formally inviting Sweden and Finland to join the alliance, Stoltenberg declared that NATO’s rapid reaction force, a collection of air, sea, and land units maintained at a state of high readiness, would increase from 40,000 troops to more than 300,000. In April 2023 Finland became the 31st member of NATO, but Sweden’s accession was held up by objections from Turkey and Hungary until March 2024, when Sweden became the alliance’s 32nd member.

high_priority_articles.title: Comment: Europe’s greenwashing paradox – could SFDR undermine EmpCo enforcement? - Responsible Investor
high_priority_articles.summary: Comment: Europe’s greenwashing paradox – could SFDR undermine EmpCo enforcement?  Responsible Investor
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Since 27 September, tougher EU consumer-protection rules have been in force against greenwashing under the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (EmpCo).
They restrict generic environmental claims, discipline claims about future environmental performance, and subject sustainability labels to tighter controls.
At the same time, Brussels is revising its Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) and creating fund categories that could give some weak sustainability claims greater authority – and make them harder to challenge.
EmpCo’s logic is straightforward: a green claim is not limited to an explicit promise. It may be conveyed by a label, product name, image, colour scheme or overall presentation – and must not mislead the average consumer.
Claims about future environmental performance require clear, objective, publicly available and verifiable commitments and targets, set out in a realistic implementation plan with measurable, time-bound targets and regular independent verification.
EmpCo also bars sustainability labels unless they are based on a certification scheme or established by a public authority.
The SFDR revision would create product categories rather than labels. But those statutory sustainability categories will function as labels in the market: public designations that private fund managers use to identify and market products.
Official categories create legitimate expectations among investors, advisers and fund selectors, and invite reliance on regulatory recognition as a substitute for scrutiny. That makes their design decisive.
European policymakers are now seeking to streamline disclosures and replace the de facto Article 8 and 9 labels with official Sustainable, Transition and ESG Basics categories backed by formal criteria: minimum investment thresholds, exclusions and specified qualifying investment routes. The proposal presents them as tools for mobilising and allocating capital towards the transition of the real economy.
“Claims about future environmental performance require clear, objective, publicly available and verifiable commitments and targets”
That makes the regulation’s interaction with EmpCo consequential. Under Article 3(4) of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD), which EmpCo amends, sector-specific EU rules prevail in the event of conflict, but only for the aspects they specifically regulate.
The European Commission’s SFDR explanatory memorandum and recital 12 expressly state that proper compliance with SFDR requirements should satisfy the corresponding UCPD consumer-protection requirements for sustainability claims within its scope.
Consumer authorities may still challenge product language that goes beyond what the rules authorise. The extent of protection will depend on how specifically the final SFDR defines a category’s meaning and permitted use.
SFDR’s greenwashing risk
If SFDR categories themselves are weak, EmpCo may be left policing the wording around official designations while their compliant use becomes harder to challenge.
That makes it all the more important to address greenwashing risk within SFDR at two levels: the credibility of the categories and the coherence of the products that use them. Neither requires reopening the architecture of the proposed regime.
The first requirement is credible categories. Formal criteria are indispensable. They provide legal certainty, comparability and observable conditions for supervision. Where those criteria remain under negotiation, they must be compatible with what category names reasonably lead investors to expect.
Consider the proposed Transition category. Under a political compromise, it could include investment in some companies developing new fossil-fuel projects if they meet certain conditions, including Taxonomy-aligned capital expenditure.
But “Transition” is likely to signal something different to a retail investor: a business moving away from fossil-fuel dependence, rather than one diversifying into clean energy while also expanding oil-and-gas supply.
“A framework intended to curb misleading sustainability claims may end up greenlighting greenwashing”
The second requirement is coherent products. Even well-designed criteria have limits. They are gatekeepers, not proof that a product coherently serves the purpose its category conveys or can plausibly contribute to the outcome it implies.
Products built around portfolio-emissions compression illustrate the point. A fund can lower weighted-average carbon metrics simply by reallocating away from carbon-intensive holdings, regardless of their issuers’ importance to the transition, their transition performance or actual decarbonisation.
That may improve the fund’s reported carbon footprint, and possibly reduce its exposure to carbon-price risk. But that alone does not show that the strategy finances the transformation of industrial sectors, rewards companies’ transition efforts, or supports decarbonisation progress.
This is not a thought experiment. Portfolio-level emissions reduction is a qualifying investment approach in the proposed SFDR revision, and underpins the EU’s official climate-benchmark standards, the use of which receives preferential treatment under the proposal.
The answer is not to prescribe one investment model. Funds may support the transition by financing specific projects or assets, investing in bonds or loans with proceeds earmarked for transition or enabling activities, allocating capital to companies making credible progress, or using stewardship and engagement to press for change. But flexibility must be matched by accountability.
Alongside formal qualification criteria, managers using an official category should have to show their work: explain and evidence, in standardised form, how the objective they pursue serves the category’s purpose; how their strategy and implementation are expected to achieve it; why their indicators are informative; and, where real-economy effects are claimed or implied, why those effects are plausible.
This would not guarantee a climate outcome, alter eligibility or exclude products that meet the formal criteria. It would add substantiation, not another investment model or eligibility test. It would give investors, advisers and fund selectors the evidence needed to distinguish credible strategies from weaker ones – and regulators a firmer basis for supervision.
ESMA’s 12 October notes on transition and impact claims point in this direction. They call for explanations linking ambitions, strategies, metrics and results, and warn against equating portfolio decarbonisation with real-economy emissions reductions or confusing investee impact with investor impact.
These notes address non-regulatory communications and create no new requirements. Their logic should inform SFDR’s statutory product requirements, including substantiation of the claims conveyed by the categories themselves.
The broader lesson is that public categories do not merely discipline private claims; they can also legitimise and shield them. When weakly designed, they give questionable claims a stronger regulatory footing. A claim may not become less misleading, but it can become more trusted, less scrutinised and harder to challenge.
As EU lawmakers finalise the rules, they should align category criteria more closely with their stated purposes and require fund managers to substantiate how their investment processes serve them. Otherwise, a framework intended to curb misleading sustainability claims may end up greenlighting greenwashing.
Frédéric Ducoulombier is programme director, climate regulation and policies, at EDHEC Climate Institute.

The 20-Year Leap: How Vietnam’s Factory-First Engine Left Indonesia Behind
Key Takeaways
| ● | Vietnam's nominal GDP per capita is projected to reach $5,259 this year, officially surpassing Indonesia's $5,153 according to latest International Monetary Fund estimates. | 
| ● | The economic inflection caps a structural divergence two decades in the making, heralded in 2005 when Vietnam's per capita electricity generation first crossed above Indonesia's. | 
| ● | High-tech manufacturing drives nearly 25% of Vietnam's economy compared to roughly 19% in Indonesia, cementing Hanoi as a premier global hub for electronics and semiconductors. | 
| ● | Indonesian business lobby Kadin has outlined an aggressive "5D" strategy and eight industry task forces to accelerate domestic competitiveness and escape the middle-income trap. | 
A multi-level highway interchange illuminates evening traffic in Ho Chi Minh City as industrial infrastructure outlays accelerate across Vietnam. Photo: VnExpress
JAKARTA, Investortrust.id — A historic economic milestone is unfolding across Southeast Asia. According to the International Monetary Fund’s October World Economic Outlook, Vietnam’s gross domestic product per capita is projected to reach $5,259 this year, eclipsing Indonesia’s $5,153. The figures represent an 8.9% year-on-year advance for Hanoi, almost doubling its nominal output per person over the past decade, while pushing Vietnam into fifth place among ASEAN members behind Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia, and Thailand.
The IMF projects Vietnam will maintain its per-capita lead into 2027, reaching $5,659 against Indonesia’s $5,550. While Indonesia remains the undisputed heavyweight of Southeast Asia in absolute terms—commanding a $1.48 trillion overall GDP against Vietnam’s $542 billion due to a population nearly three times larger—the per-person inversion marks a watershed realignment for the region’s balance of economic momentum.
Per capita income is the ultimate barometer of national productivity and living standards. For decades, Indonesia stood comfortably ahead of Vietnam, holding an estimated $250 lead as recently as last year. That Vietnam has leapfrogged the archipelago underscores how relentlessly focused industrial policy, trade openness, and aggressive capital deepening can outflank a resource-rich domestic consumption giant. As multilateral institutions forecast Vietnam's economy to expand 8.4% this year alongside a blazing 9.95% third-quarter print, Indonesia's steady 5% trajectory is proving insufficient to defend its regional hierarchy.
A Divergence Twenty Years in the Making
While headline observers treat the 2026 per-capita flip as a sudden development, the underlying shift has been two decades in the making.
Data on industrial energy consumption shows that Vietnam’s annual per capita electricity generation first crossed above Indonesia’s back in 2005. That subtle inflection signaled that Vietnam had begun electrifying and equipping its workforce at a far more aggressive velocity. Over the subsequent twenty years, Vietnam’s power buildout climbed almost vertically, surging from parity to over 3,000 kilowatt-hours per person by 2024, more than double Indonesia's generation rate.
Because electricity consumption in developing economies tracks factory tooling, automated assembly lines, and industrial capacity, Vietnam’s surging grid was the advance indicator of its factory-first transformation. While Indonesia’s per capita power growth climbed at an incremental incline, Vietnam was building the generation capacity necessary to power continuous shifts of high-tech production.
Factory Floor vs. Commodity Vault
The root of Hanoi's per-capita ascent lies in the sheer manufacturing intensity of its economy. Manufacturing value-added accounts for roughly 25% of Vietnam's GDP, acting as the primary engine of national expansion. When including the broader industry and construction envelope, that footprint accounts for nearly 37% to 44% of total output.
By comparison, manufacturing’s contribution to Indonesia's gross domestic product has dwindled from approximately 32% in 2002 to roughly 19% today. Instead of scaling high-tech factory floors, Indonesia rode successive commodity booms across coal and palm oil, leaving its economy anchored by extractive primary sectors and low-productivity informal services.
Vietnam capitalized on global supply chain realignments, embedding itself directly into Tier-1 multinational production networks. Global titans such as Taiwan’s Foxconn and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics turned northern Vietnam into a dominant production base for smartphones, semiconductors, and precision components. Supported by an expansive public investment push totaling VND 1.014 quadrillion ($39.3 billion) this year for highways, ports, and airports, Vietnam is targeting full-year growth of at least 10% on its way toward an $8,500 per capita milestone by 2030.
Indonesia Counters With Reindustrialization Drive
Despite Vietnam's milestone, Indonesian business leaders and policymakers insist that the nation's economic potential remains unmatched if it can successfully execute structural reindustrialization.
Addressing delegates at the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin) National Leadership Meeting (Rapimnas) in Jakarta on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, Kadin Chairman Anindya Novyan Bakrie emphasized that the business community is actively building economic shock absorbers while mounting a nationwide competitiveness campaign.
"We do not see this as a crisis, but it is a formidable challenge," Bakrie told reporters, noting that corporate balance sheets and household purchasing power must be protected through close coordination between the private sector and the central government.
Bakrie underscored that 92% of Indonesia's gross domestic product is generated outside the central government budget, making private enterprise and industrial execution the definitive arbiters of long-term wealth. To reclaim momentum, Kadin is spearheading an operational "5D" strategy centered on fiscal discipline and decentralization, aggressive deregulation, operational debottlenecking, sovereign capital deployment through investment agency Danantara, and systematic capacity upgrades for micro, small, and medium enterprises.
To prevent plans from stalling in rhetoric, Kadin has established eight specialized task forces evaluated on rolling quarterly performance cycles, targeting supply-chain integration, mineral downstreaming, human capital productivity, and energy sovereignty. Bakrie introduced the twin national rallying cries of "Buy Indonesia" to draw patient direct investment into physical capacity, and "Buy from Indonesia" to integrate domestic producers into 77 premier global supplier networks spanning aerospace to electric transport.
Bakrie concluded that the ultimate goal is converting Indonesia's historic crisis endurance into proactive global competitiveness, presenting the chamber's roadmap directly to President Prabowo Subianto.
"Indonesia’s resilience has been tested and proven across generations," Bakrie said. "What we must now step forward and deliver is our competitiveness."

India, Mexico formally begin preferential trade agreement negotiations
The proposed agreement will cover market access, rules of origin, customs procedures and trade remedies as India looks to deepen its trade footprint in Latin America
Listen to This Article
India and Mexico have launched negotiations for a preferential trade agreement (PTA) after signing the terms of reference (ToR) for the proposed deal, the Department of Commerce said on Wednesday.
“The signing formally launches negotiations for a mutually beneficial and balanced PTA, with the potential to expand bilateral trade, create business opportunities, enhance investment flows and contribute to resilient and diversified supply chains,” the department said in a press release.
The signing of the ToR and launch of negotiations were part of Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal’s two-day visit to Mexico City, which began on Tuesday.
The two sides had finalised the ToR more than three months ago and were awaiting an appropriate time to schedule the visit and formal signing.
“During the visit of Commerce Secretary, Rajesh Agrawal, both delegations discussed bilateral relations and opportunities to expand trade and investment flows,” the release said.

“The discussions were held with Mexico’s Undersecretary of Foreign Trade, Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez Romano, who participated on behalf of Secretary of Economy Marcelo Ebrard Casaubon.”
The ToR for a trade agreement serves as a formal roadmap setting out the boundaries, objectives, scope and rules before official negotiations begin.
The India-Mexico ToR covers key negotiating areas, including market access for goods, rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, dispute settlement, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade and trade remedies.
The proposed deal seeks to leverage complementarities between the two economies and expand opportunities for Mexican products and businesses in the Indian market.
“With its strong linkages to global value chains, Mexico is an important market for Indian exporters and investors. Sectors with significant potential for cooperation include automotive, chemicals, electronics, pharmaceuticals, agri-food, energy, critical minerals, medical devices, and advanced manufacturing, among others,” the release said.
New Delhi initiated discussions for a trade agreement with Mexico after the latter imposed tariffs of as much as 50 per cent on more than 1,400 products from non-preferential trading partners, including India.
Despite the tariffs, India’s exports to Mexico have grown nearly 26 per cent so far in the current financial year through August, according to the latest data available with the Department of Commerce.
India exported goods worth $5.73 billion to Mexico in 2025-26 (FY26), with nearly half of the shipments comprising vehicles and auto components, and electrical machinery and equipment.
India recorded a trade surplus of $3.63 billion with Mexico during the year.
The proposed agreement with Mexico is part of India’s broader strategy to diversify export markets and expand its footprint in Latin America.
The Department of Commerce is also engaged in trade agreement negotiations with other economies in the region, including Chile and Peru, as well as the Brazil-led five-member Mercosur bloc.

Logistics Update
Trends to Watch
Talking Tariffs
- Section 338 Product List for Canada Gets Reshuffled Again, With New Duties Starting October 30: An October 23 presidential action changes which Canadian goods face Section 338 duties, and the new list applies to entries on or after October 30. A total of 22 tariff lines come off, among them plywood, plastic wrap, cardboard boxes, and food-related machinery, while about 100 go on, including cocoa products, carpets and other floor coverings, wood panels, coatings, air conditioning units, and some recreational goods.
  - The timing matters for anything in transit: a chest-type freezer, for example, owes only Section 232 steel duties on entries through October 29 and then picks up Section 338 duties on top beginning October 30, while plywood moves the other way and stops attracting the 50% Section 338 rate after October 29, per Flexport’s Tariff Simulator.
  - The duties stack on top of Section 232 tariffs and apply whether or not a product qualifies for U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) treatment.
  - This is the second round of list changes since mid-September, when cheese, hides, motorboats, and other items were added and a few large-format spirits were dropped. It also lands while the first lawsuit challenging the tariffs works its way through the Court of International Trade.
  - Importers moving Canadian-origin goods should re-run classification against the new annex before shipments land, since the list has shifted in both directions. The Tariff Simulator already reflects the updated product list.
- Wind Turbines Get a Negotiation Track Rather Than New Section 232 Tariffs: An October 22 proclamation closes out the Section 232 investigation into wind turbines without adding a new tariff. The Commerce Department found that turbines and their components pose a national security risk, citing remote-access weaknesses in imported inverters, radar interference, and strain on the electrical grid, and President Donald Trump agreed, but he directed Commerce and the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to negotiate with trading partners and report back within 180 days instead of imposing duties.
  - Existing Section 232 duties aren’t touched. Turbine components made of steel, aluminum, or copper still pay the tariffs already in place on those metals, and the proclamation states that it doesn’t modify them.
  - Other remedies stay available depending on how the negotiations go, and the 180-day update comes due around April 20, 2027.
  - Importers of turbines and turbine components should keep classification and metal-content records current, since the existing metals duties continue to apply to those parts in the meantime.
- Robotics and Industrial Machinery Imports Get a Negotiation Mandate Instead of Tariffs, With a 180-Day Check-In: The Section 232 investigation into robotics and industrial machinery ended with a finding but no new duties. Commerce concluded that the amount of robots, factory equipment, and parts coming in from abroad is a national security risk, and the President agreed in an October 28 proclamation, yet the remedy he chose for now is diplomacy: Commerce and USTR are to work out agreements with exporting countries and report back within 180 days.
  - Tariffs aren’t off the table for good. The proclamation says the President may revisit duties, quotas, and fees, or set up an incentive program for new U.S. production of robotics and machinery, depending on how the talks go, and he can act sooner if no agreement materializes within the 180 days.
  - The administration’s reasoning leans on import dependence and data security. The U.S. relies on foreign sources for most types of robotics and industrial equipment, and the proclamation flags cybersecurity weaknesses in imported systems that sit inside manufacturing and defense operations.
  - Importers of industrial equipment should plan around a decision window that closes in late April 2027, when the robotics update comes due, rather than assume the question is settled.
- Latest UFLPA Entity List Update Takes the Roster to 190 Companies: Screening suppliers against the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List is about to take a bit longer: the roster is heading to 190 companies, up three, after the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) named additional businesses with ties to Xinjiang in a Federal Register notice.
  - Goods made wholly or in part by a listed entity are presumed to involve forced labor and are blocked from entry unless the importer shows with clear and convincing evidence that they don’t.
  - The presumption reaches inputs as well as finished goods, so U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) can detain a shipment that contains material from a listed company several tiers upstream, even when the direct supplier isn’t on the list.
  - Importers should screen their supplier and sub-tier supplier lists against the updated roster now. The Federal Register notice carries the three added names and their effective date, and Flexport’s Trade Advisory group can help importers work through a UFLPA detention if one occurs.
TRANS-PACIFIC EASTBOUND (TPEB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Carriers deployed record capacity during Golden Week, with weekly Asia-to-U.S. West Coast capacity at 393,000 TEU compared with a normal level below 300,000 TEU.
  - Delayed vessels bunched together and sailed as “double sailings,” which canceled out planned blank sailings.
  - With the winter slack season starting, carriers are matching capacity to softer demand to protect rates, rather than responding to a demand-driven squeeze.
- Freight Rates:
  - Trans-Pacific rates remain above Asia-Europe levels, but the planned November 1 rate increase faces pressure as carriers compete for volume.
  - The U.S. has also proposed extending its suspension of added port fees on China-linked vessels to January 9, 2027. The current suspension expires November 10.
  - Shippers should add buffer to cargo-ready dates out of Shanghai and Ningbo for the next few weeks and avoid relying on a single sailing.
FAR EAST WESTBOUND (FEWB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Blank sailings are 8.1% this week, with 3.4% next week and a range of 4.8-11.4% through November.
  - Overall deployed capacity to Northern Europe is still expected to reach a record level, so the blanks reflect carriers managing utilization against excess supply, rather than a space shortage.
- Suez Canal Return:
  - Capacity continues to shift back to standard Suez Canal routing. About 63% of Far East-to-Europe deployed capacity now sails via Suez: 70% on Far East to Mediterranean and 58% on Far East to Northern Europe.
  - MSC resumed Suez transits in August. The Gemini Cooperation of Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd began returning services in Q3, and Maersk aims to return all services by March 2027.
  - CMA CGM kept a Suez presence throughout, and Ocean Alliance has restored 6 services.
  - Premier Alliance has announced returns, while ZIM has not resumed. Some carriers keep selected Cape of Good Hope services as a hedge.
  - Shorter transit times are an option on part of the network, though the shift is happening carrier by carrier, even vessel by vessel, so shippers should confirm routing at booking.
  - Ships returning to Suez are also arriving alongside vessels still sailing around the Cape, which adds port congestion.
- Freight Rates:
  - Rates on the main Shanghai-to-Northern Europe index were unchanged week over week.
  - Carriers’ November 1 rate increase is unlikely to hold as supply outpaces demand. The situation will continue to be monitored.
TRANS-ATLANTIC WESTBOUND (TAWB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Blank sailings are 7.9% this week, then range from 0% to ~9% over the next 4 weeks. Offered capacity stays 5-16% below standard in most weeks, and selective NEUR-US East/Gulf blanks continue (~5% cancellations).
  - Vessel utilization is above 93% out of NEUR and WMED, so capacity is largely deployed.
- Operations:
  - Schedule reliability for the largest carrier networks was only 68-69% in August and September, against a 90% goal for the largest network.
  - Yards remain tight in Rotterdam, Bremerhaven and Hamburg, and container/chassis availability is limited at inland origins. Shippers should book 3-4 weeks ahead and build extra time between cargo-ready dates and vessel cutoffs.
- Freight Rates:
  - The winter slack season and added capacity from the Suez return point to continued pressure on rates. The Suez return is gradual and partial, so the effect on TAWB is likely indirect and slower than on Asia-Europe.
  - The situation will continue to be monitored.
INDIAN SUBCONTINENT TO NORTH AMERICA
- Capacity and Demand:
  - The Indian Subcontinent to the US extended Peak Season is experiencing downward market pressure leading into the Diwali Holiday in India in November.
  - Port congestion and vessel bunching across South and Southeast Asia continue to absorb effective capacity but have shown improvement at key regional hubs Nhava Sheva, Colombo, and Mundra.
  - Space on the major service strings ISC to USEC has begun to become more available.
  - Origin lead times for getting loaded on time demonstrate further normalization in the market.
  - Shippers should continue to book early, allow extra time at origin ports, and confirm routing options for urgent cargo.
- Freight Rates:
  - Market rate levels have reduced for back-to-back validity periods for major lanes ISC to USEC, and rates ISC to the WC have begun to soften.

high_priority_articles.title: India-US Trade Agreement in Final Stages, but Challenges Remain, Jaishankar Says - INDIA New England News
high_priority_articles.summary: India-US Trade Agreement in Final Stages, but Challenges Remain, Jaishankar Says  INDIA New England News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI — India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said Thursday that negotiations over a proposed trade agreement between India and the United States have entered their final stages, although unresolved issues remain and a deal cannot be considered complete until both sides formally reach an agreement.
Speaking at the NDTV World Summit in New Delhi, Jaishankar described the negotiations as being in the “last mile,” reflecting growing expectations that the two countries are approaching a breakthrough in their long-running trade discussions.
He said recent statements by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal also suggested that the negotiations were nearing completion.
“What you’ve heard not just from Secretary Rubio, but from Minister Piyush Goyal, from others, from me, is that we are moving towards it,” Jaishankar said.
However, he cautioned against assuming that an agreement was inevitable before the remaining differences were resolved.
“Well, look, it’s never done till it’s done,” he said.
Jaishankar acknowledged that the final stages of trade negotiations can be particularly difficult, even when the parties have reached broad agreement on major issues.
“Often the last mile or the penultimate miles do pose their challenges. I think the [negotiating] teams are working through them now,” he said.
When asked about the specific obstacles preventing a final agreement, the foreign minister declined to disclose details, emphasizing that resolving those differences was the responsibility of the negotiating teams.
“If you’re asking me to tell you what exactly those challenges are, I’m sorry I won’t. That’s for the negotiators to sort out,” he added.
The comments come amid renewed diplomatic engagement between New Delhi and Washington, with senior officials from both countries expressing optimism about strengthening economic ties.
A bilateral trade agreement is widely viewed as an important step toward expanding commercial relations between the world’s two largest democracies.
Both governments have been working to deepen cooperation in areas including trade, energy, technology and defense, while addressing longstanding commercial differences.
Jaishankar’s remarks followed his recent meeting with Rubio in Mumbai, where the two leaders discussed bilateral priorities and regional developments.
According to the U.S. State Department, the talks included energy security, defense cooperation and developments in West Asia.
“The secretary reiterated that increased energy trade with the United States can play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand,” the State Department said.
Rubio also welcomed progress in bilateral defense and civil nuclear cooperation and encouraged India to increase purchases of American technology and defense systems.
The discussions underscored Washington’s interest in expanding its role as a supplier of energy, advanced technologies and defense equipment to India.
U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who attended the meeting, described the discussions as “productive” and highlighted the growing momentum behind cooperation in several strategic sectors.
Gor said the talks focused on strengthening ties in defense, energy, emerging technologies and trade as the two countries seek to advance their broader strategic partnership.
The renewed diplomatic activity has added to expectations that a trade agreement could be finalized soon, although neither government has announced a signing date.
Jaishankar’s comments suggest that while negotiations have made substantial progress, both sides remain focused on resolving outstanding differences before making a formal announcement.
For now, the Indian government maintains that the agreement is moving closer to completion, with negotiators continuing their efforts to bridge the remaining gaps. (Source: IANS)

high_priority_articles.title: Chile urges U.S. to widen tariff exemptions on exports hit by a 12.5% surcharge - Vinetur
high_priority_articles.summary: Chile urges U.S. to widen tariff exemptions on exports hit by a 12.5% surcharge  Vinetur
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The latest talks ended without a deal, leaving wine producers and other exporters exposed to higher costs
Friday, October 30, 2026
Chile’s government said it met with the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Thursday, October 29, to press for broader exemptions from a 12.5% tariff surcharge that is affecting part of the country’s exports to the United States.
The meeting brought together Paula Estévez, Chile’s undersecretary for international economic relations, and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during Estévez’s visit to the United States. According to the Chilean government, she used the talks to restate Chile’s case for removing more products from the surcharge and to push for trading conditions that support bilateral commerce.
Chile said products that are already exempt account for 53.6% of the country’s shipments, but Santiago wants that share to grow. No new tariff agreement was announced after the meeting, and the negotiations remain open.
The latest talks are part of a longer bilateral effort that Chile says has been underway since the first half of 2025, after the Trump administration’s initial tariff announcements. Chile’s goal since then has been to preserve the best possible access for its exporters to the U.S. market, which officials describe as one of the country’s most important overseas destinations.
In comments released by the Chilean government, Estévez said the United States had changed its trade policy and was now negotiating bilateral arrangements with several countries after imposing tariffs on all of its trading partners. She said Chile was acting pragmatically to secure the best conditions it could for local exporters.
Estévez also said the Thursday, October 29, meeting was useful because it allowed Chile to reinforce its position directly with U.S. officials. She repeated Chile’s opposition to tariffs and said more Chilean products should be exempt. She added that Chile remained open to what she described as a pragmatic, mutually beneficial solution.
The meeting followed the most recent previous negotiating round in August, when a U.S. delegation led by Deputy USTR Jeffrey Goettman traveled to Chile. The October 29 contact signaled that both sides are still engaged, even though they have not yet announced a breakthrough.
The tariff dispute matters beyond Chile’s broader export sector because any expansion of exemptions could have direct effects on beverage trade. Wine is among the Chilean products exposed to the 12.5% surcharge, and any relief would likely improve the position of Chilean producers in the U.S. market. Lower duties could also change competitive conditions among imported wines and other beverage categories by affecting retail pricing, margins, and the relative appeal of different origins.
That makes the talks especially important for Chile’s wine industry, which relies heavily on export markets and has long treated the United States as a key destination. For importers, distributors, and retailers in the U.S., the outcome could influence sourcing decisions if tariff costs remain in place or are reduced for some products and not for others.
The Chilean government did not provide a detailed list of the products discussed in the latest meeting, nor did it say whether the two sides had narrowed their differences on specific goods. Its statement focused instead on Chile’s general effort to widen the pool of exempt products and maintain favorable access to the American market.
The October 29 meeting took place during a U.S. visit linked to the program “Navigating the Global Trade Reset: Strategic Options for Latin America and the Caribbean,” organized by the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean and the Georgetown Americas Institute. Chile said the trip also included meetings with other U.S. officials on the broader economic relationship between the two countries.
According to the Chilean government, Estévez’s agenda in the United States included talks with Juan Pablo Segura at the State Department and with senior Commerce Department officials responsible for industry and security and for international trade. Those meetings also centered on economic ties between Chile and the United States, underscoring that the tariff issue is being handled alongside a wider set of commercial and strategic discussions.

high_priority_articles.title: Qatar’s LNG Empire Is Being Strangled by the War with Iran - Todayville
high_priority_articles.summary: Qatar’s LNG Empire Is Being Strangled by the War with Iran  Todayville
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The wealth of the Gulf states depends upon their ability to export energy to the rest of the world. Qatar is a particularly dangerous case because its economy depends heavily upon liquefied natural gas (LNG), and nearly all of that export trade must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar’s LNG exports had collapsed by 96% by the end of August. The country lost an estimated $24 billion in gas sales during the first six months of the conflict, equivalent to approximately five months of its 2025 gas income. This is an extraordinary loss for a nation that has built its wealth upon supplying energy to the global economy.
The situation has become so desperate that QatarEnergy, once one of the world’s dominant LNG exporters, is now purchasing American natural gas to fulfill its international obligations. QatarEnergy has reportedly entered into a 30-year agreement with Cheniere Energy to purchase 4 million metric tons of LNG annually through 2054, with deliveries expected to begin in the 2030s. The company is also negotiating with Venture Global for another 3 million tons annually. Qatar possesses one of the largest natural gas reserves on the planet, yet it is arranging to buy LNG from its American competitors because it cannot reliably deliver its own product to customers. The country has not run out of gas. It has lost reliable access to the shipping routes necessary to sell it.
Iranian attacks have compounded the disaster. Two production trains at Qatar’s Ras Laffan complex were damaged, removing approximately 17% of the country’s LNG export capacity. Repairs could take three years. The remaining production capacity is of limited economic value if the tankers cannot safely reach international markets. QatarEnergy has repeatedly declared force majeure on supply contracts, leaving customers in Asia and Europe scrambling for replacement shipments. Qatar had exported only 18 LNG cargoes through the end of August, compared with 509 during the same period in 2025. Those numbers demonstrate how thoroughly the conflict disrupted one of the world’s most important energy suppliers.
The geographical problem is especially severe. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates possess oil pipelines that can move some crude production toward ports outside the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar does not enjoy that flexibility. Natural gas cannot simply be loaded onto an ordinary tanker or pumped through an existing crude oil pipeline. LNG requires specialized liquefaction facilities, storage infrastructure, and vessels capable of maintaining extremely low temperatures. Constructing an alternative export system across Saudi Arabia or the UAE would require enormous investment, new infrastructure, and political agreements, none of which would provide immediate relief. Qatar is effectively trapped by its geography. Its principal source of national income depends upon a maritime passage that Iran can threaten at any moment.
This is precisely why I have emphasized the sovereign debt problems developing throughout the Middle East. Governments have built spending commitments around the assumption that energy revenues will continue flowing. Qatar has accumulated substantial financial reserves and overseas investments, which provide it with more protection than many other countries. Nevertheless, reserves are not an unlimited substitute for income. The government still has to finance public services, infrastructure, salaries, subsidies, and existing obligations while its principal export industry struggles to operate. The longer the disruption continues, the more pressure there will be to postpone spending, reconsider investment commitments, and conserve available liquidity.
Qatar recorded a budget deficit of approximately $5.8 billion in the second quarter of 2026, its largest quarterly shortfall in nearly a decade. LNG exports fell from roughly 20 million tons per quarter before the war to less than 2 million tons between April and June. Government revenues dropped approximately 30%, while expenditures declined only 2.6%.
Nonessential construction, discretionary spending, and projects that don’t contribute directly to economic survival become harder to justify. Qatar has spent decades transforming its energy wealth into enormous infrastructure projects, international investments, and an expanding global presence. That model works exceptionally well when LNG revenues arrive without interruption. When the primary source of income is suddenly restricted, the government must reassess how long it can sustain its commitments. There is no indication that every nonessential project has been canceled, but the financial incentive to delay discretionary expenditures is unmistakable.
The consequences are also being felt throughout Asia and Europe. India, Bangladesh, and other major LNG importers have been forced to seek alternative supplies, while European gas storage remains vulnerable ahead of winter. Qatar previously supplied approximately one-fifth of global LNG trade. Removing that volume from international markets does not simply hurt Qatar. It creates competition for the remaining available gas, increases transportation and insurance costs, and places additional pressure on countries that depend upon imported energy. Europe has already undermined its industrial competitiveness through expensive energy policies and its confrontation with Russia. Another prolonged disruption to natural gas supplies will only make matters worse.
Qatar is far from bankrupt, and it possesses substantial financial assets that can help it endure this crisis. But there is a tremendous difference between possessing wealth and generating the income required to sustain an economy. A nation cannot indefinitely finance its obligations by drawing down reserves while its primary export industry remains constrained. Qatar has begun restoring some LNG shipments through Hormuz, but those voyages remain vulnerable to renewed attacks. Even a partial recovery does not eliminate the problem when the entire economic structure depends upon safe passage through one narrow waterway.
I have maintained that the Middle East War Cycle would have consequences far beyond the battlefield. Qatar demonstrates how a country can become an economic casualty of a war even when it is not the principal combatant. The government has little choice but to conserve its financial resources, protect its remaining energy infrastructure, and hope that shipping conditions improve before the damage becomes permanent. Its enormous gas reserves have not disappeared, but those reserves cannot pay the bills if they cannot reach the customer. The longer this conflict continues, the more governments throughout the region will discover that their financial security was built upon assumptions about peace and uninterrupted trade that no longer hold.

Manufacturers could gain access to larger regional markets.
Logistics and transportation companies may benefit from increased cross-border goods movement.
Banks and payment providers could support additional trade financing, business payments, and corporate investment.
Agricultural businesses may also gain from improved regional supply chains and market access.

Implementation requires cooperation across national governments and regulatory bodies.
Border infrastructure, customs procedures, transportation networks, and non-tariff barriers remain important obstacles.
Investors should distinguish between the agreement’s long-term potential and reforms already implemented.

high_priority_articles.title: Nigeria’s API Production Can Boost Non-oil Exports, African Trade – FG - News Agency of Nigeria
high_priority_articles.summary: Nigeria’s API Production Can Boost Non-oil Exports, African Trade – FG  News Agency of Nigeria
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By Folasade Akpan
The Federal Government says Nigeria can become a regional supplier of pharmaceutical ingredients, deepen African pharmaceutical value chains and boost its non-oil exports if it develops the capacity to produce them competitively.
Dr Chris Isokpunwu, the Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, said this on Friday in Abuja at the Future of Health Conference 2026, organised by Nigeria Health Watch in collaboration with the World Bank Group, in Abuja.
The meeting has “Accelerating the Shift to Domestic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients Production for Priority Essential Medicines in Nigeria,” as theme.
Isokpunwu said Nigeria had the market, population and entrepreneurial capacity to develop a competitive pharmaceutical manufacturing industry.
He said that the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) also offered an opportunity to expand the market for locally manufactured pharmaceutical inputs.
“With the right production capacity and internationally competitive standards, Nigeria can position itself as a regional supplier of pharmaceutical inputs, deepen African value chains and strengthen its non-oil industrial exports,” he said.
He, however, said achieving this would require deliberate identification of priority essential medicines, assessment of the technical and commercial feasibility of local production and a phased approach to attracting credible investors.
He described domestic production of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) as a strategic imperative connecting public health, industrialisation, investment, trade and national security.
“Nigeria cannot achieve sustainable health security while remaining heavily dependent on external sources for critical pharmaceutical inputs,” he said.
According to him, local API production would strengthen medicine supply chains, reduce exposure to international disruptions and foreign exchange pressures, create skilled employment and retain more value within the Nigerian economy.
He identified predictable policies, an enabling regulatory environment, reliable power and other infrastructure, affordable financing and a sustainable market as essential conditions for attracting investment into local API manufacturing.
The permanent secretary said government also needed to support technology transfer, skills development, research and industrial partnerships, alongside effective coordination among relevant ministries and regulatory institutions.
He recalled that the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment had initiated the establishment of the Health Industries Corporation of Nigeria (HICON) to catalyse investment in APIs, basic medical hardware, pharmaceutical products, herbal medicines and diagnostic devices.
On his part, Dr Abdul Muktar, National Coordinator, Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC), said the initiative was working with the private sector to identify and prioritise APIs according to Nigeria’s public health needs.
Represented by Dr Zara Abba-Aji, he said PVAC was also collaborating with the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA) on excipient manufacturing.
He noted that domestic pharmaceutical production required a holistic approach involving access to capital, workforce development and affordable medicines.
Muktar said the initiative was working with a local manufacturer to facilitate access to European Investment Bank (EIB) funding and technical expertise for manufacturing and technology transfer.
He described the federal government’s 2024 Executive Order, which provided local manufacturers access to precursor ingredients, including APIs, as a temporary measure towards achieving domestic production.
Also speaking, Dr Olumide Okunola of the World Bank Group and International Finance Corporation (IFC) said pharmaceutical manufacturing presented significant health and economic opportunities for Nigeria.
He said investments in the health economy could improve health outcomes, increase productivity, create jobs and strengthen national competitiveness.
Okunola cited a modelling report which estimated that developing Nigeria’s health economy could unlock more than 40 billion dollars in value, equivalent to nearly eight per cent of the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
He said Nigeria had about 200 pharmaceutical manufacturers, but their production capacity remained below 40 per cent due to challenges including regulation, inadequate power supply and financing constraints.
“Each and every single one of them needs to go to China, India to import their APIs even to make paracetamol,” he said.
Okunola said Nigeria could leverage its petrochemical infrastructure to develop domestic API production, while strategically identifying products that offered the greatest economic and health security value.
He also commended the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) for developing an API policy, describing it as an important first step towards establishing a foundation for domestic production.
In her remarks, the Managing Director, Nigeria Health Watch, Vivianne Ihekweazu, said Nigeria’s dependence on imported pharmaceutical ingredients exposed its medicine supply chain to foreign exchange fluctuations and international disruptions.
She said the COVID-19 pandemic had demonstrated the vulnerability of countries that depended on external sources for essential medicines and other health supplies.
Ihekweazu said the conference was focusing on how Nigeria could strengthen its capacity to manufacture the ingredients required for essential medicines, adding that medicine security was an important component of health system resilience.
She said access to affordable medicines remained a major concern, noting that local production could help address cost pressures associated with imported ingredients.
She called for coordinated action by the ministries of health and industry, regulators, financial institutions and the private sector to create an enabling environment for sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing.
Similarly, the Chief Executive Officer, Bloom Public Health, Prof. Chimezie Anyakora, said Nigeria had reached a stage where it should move beyond manufacturing finished pharmaceutical products to producing its active ingredients.
He said the country had developed considerable capacity in medicine manufacturing and should now advance further along the pharmaceutical value chain.
“Nigeria is among the biggest consumption and manufacturing countries in Africa. We need to be among those that will move to API manufacturing,” he said.
Anyakora said the transition would require specialised skills and urged universities to prepare professionals for the emerging area of pharmaceutical production.
He commended local manufacturers investing in API production, saying more companies needed to embrace the process.
He also called for greater public participation in ensuring medicine quality, noting that the responsibility of combating fake and substandard medicines should not rest solely with NAFDAC.
